members.statement: The goal of architecture is to minimize the human resources required to build and maintain the system; judge design quality by whether the effort to meet customer needs stays low across the whole lifetime, and treat the decisions that are expensive to change as the architecturally significant ones.

Prioritize the important architecture over urgent-but-unimportant features, and have the development team assert architecture's importance and fight for it as stakeholders, because business managers cannot evaluate it and a system whose architecture comes last becomes ever more costly until change is impossible.

Understand architecture as the shape of the system (its components, their arrangement, and how they communicate) whose primary purpose is to facilitate development, deployment, operation, and maintenance rather than merely to make the system work, ultimately to minimize lifetime cost and maximize programmer productivity.

Treat architecture as the art of drawing boundaries that defer decisions and keep them from polluting core business logic, recognizing that coupling to premature decisions — choices of frameworks, databases, web servers, libraries, and dependency injection unrelated to business requirements — saps people-power and can multiply development effort enormously, while remembering the error is premature adoption of a service or tool suite, not services themselves.

Do not mistake services for architecture: architecture is defined by the boundaries that separate high-level policy from low-level detail and follow the Dependency Rule, not by the physical mechanisms of communication, so services that merely separate behaviors are expensive function calls — still useful across processes and platforms but not architecturally significant in themselves.

Treat every architecture choice as a trade-off: there are no universally right answers, only trade-offs, so analyze the good, bad, and ugly of each option (including its downsides) instead of making value judgements about technologies.
Define and assess an architecture by all four parts — structure, architecture characteristics, architecture decisions, and design principles — not by its style/structure alone.
Distinguish architecture decisions (hard rules) from design principles (guidelines), and break a decision only through a formal, justified variance approved by a governing body.
Make architecture an engineering discipline emphasizing why over how: capture the reasoning and trade-offs behind decisions, since why is more important than how.
Recognize that every architecture is a product of its context and that data is an integral architectural concern coupled to code.

Apply architectural thinking across its four aspects: architecture-vs-design collaboration, breadth with some depth, trade-off reconciliation, and translating business drivers into architectural concerns.

Make defining, discovering, and analyzing architecture characteristics a core responsibility, calling them 'architecture characteristics' and admitting only attributes that meet all three criteria: non-domain, structurally influential, and critical to success.
Choose the fewest architecture characteristics a system needs and aim for the least-worst architecture, because characteristics interact and over-specifying is as damaging as under-specifying.

Make architecture decisions deliberately — gather information, justify technically and for the business, document, and communicate — overcoming the Covering-Your-Assets (decide at the last responsible moment, collaborate to confirm implementability), Groundhog-Day (record technical + business justification), and Email-Driven (single linked system of record, notify only the impacted) anti-patterns; treat a technology choice as an architecture decision when it supports a characteristic.

Treat architecture as changeable rather than cast in stone, and adopt continuous integration, test-driven development, and refactoring so you can revisit architectural decisions, because you will need to change them.
Recognize that tools affect architecture: ideally choose tools to fit your architecture, but in practice you often must match your architecture to the tools you have.
Design for scalability from the beginning for the parts that will need it: size for current demand but architect so growth needs no application or architectural redesign.
Focus architecture effort on decision-making and trade-off reasoning rather than implementation details, because the foundational structural decisions are the ones hardest to change later.
Keep architecture and design as separate but related activities, and reason about why an option has better trade-offs before deciding how to implement it.
Treat the architecture as the deliberate bridge from business goals to the delivered system, and design, analyze, and document it with known repeatable techniques rather than ad hoc intuition.

Deliberately design and evaluate the architecture rather than letting it be chosen by trial and error, because every system has an architecture whether or not it is known, and the architecture can support or hinder the system's important requirements.

Work on and document only the architectural structures that give insight and leverage into the system's most important quality attributes, justifying each by its return on investment; smaller systems warrant fewer structures.

Base the architecture on a prioritized list of well-specified quality attribute requirements and treat getting those right as more important than functionality, since any functionality can be met by many architectures but qualities are largely determined by the architecture.

Give the architecture conceptual integrity by making it the product of a single architect or a small group with an identified technical leader, kept in strong connection with the development team to avoid impractical ivory-tower designs.

Design so that the most common anticipated changes are local (confined to one element), because an effective architecture is one in which frequent changes are cheap, and modifiability is economically dominant given that roughly 80 percent of total system cost is incurred after deployment.

Focus architectural attention per quality attribute: manage time, shared resources, and inter-element communication for performance; assign responsibilities and limit coupling for modifiability; protect communication and control information access for security; localize resource use and avoid hard-coded limits for scalability.

Predict and check quality attributes from the architecture early instead of building, testing, and hoping, because certain architectural decisions lead to certain qualities; but remember architecture alone cannot guarantee quality, since downstream design and coding can undermine it.

Recognize that the architecture's broadest decomposition becomes engraved in the project's work-breakdown structure and organization (Conway's law), so analyze a large system's architecture before settling on a choice, because once responsibilities are formalized it is very costly to change.

Treat the architecture as a set of constraints on implementers: an implementation conforms only if it contains the prescribed elements, has them interact as prescribed, and has each fulfill its prescribed responsibilities, including decomposed per-unit performance budgets.

Analyze an architecture's ability to provide a quality attribute at any maturity stage using a tactics-based questionnaire, recording for each tactic whether it is supported, the design decisions and code location realizing it, the risk, and the rationale, scaling confidence to artifact maturity.

Know that architectures exist to satisfy requirements (the properties whose absence would make the system a failure), and focus on architecturally significant requirements (ASRs) — those whose absence would make the architecture dramatically different — which often but not always take the form of difficult, important quality attribute requirements.

Begin architecting while requirements are still in flux rather than waiting, and treat untestable quality goals such as 'be modular' or 'be highly usable' not as requirements but as invitations to start a conversation about what the requirement really is.

Recognize that architectural decisions are made with imperfect knowledge, and use a Value of Information analysis to decide how much to spend on experiments such as prototypes, weighing the cost of being wrong and the confidence gained against the team's risk appetite.

Treat architecture evaluation as a risk-reduction activity that determines fitness for purpose by analyzing alternatives and identifying the risky portions, keeping the cost of evaluation (preparation, execution, follow-up time) below the value it provides, and remembering fixing identified risks is a separate cost/benefit decision.

Base every evaluation on architectural drivers (primarily high-priority quality attribute scenarios, not functional use cases), conduct it whenever a coherent reviewable architecture exists, and at minimum have reviewers understand the architecture, determine the drivers, judge each scenario, and capture potential problems for follow-up.

Design the best architectures consciously with skilled architects rather than expecting them to emerge from self-organizing teams, write down interfaces, protocols, and structures rather than relying on face-to-face conversation alone (especially for the maintenance phase), and recognize that rapid evolution and incremental implementation require intentional up-front architecture even under enterprise-scale Agile frameworks like SAFe.

Improve organizational architecture competence — the ability to grow, use, and sustain architecture-centric practices at acceptable cost aligned with business goals — through personnel practices (career track, prestige, mentoring, training), process practices (organization-wide practices, clear authority, a review board, milestones, quality tracking, life-cycle influence), and technology practices (repositories of reusable architectures, design concepts, and tools), and probe these when interviewing.
Judge whether real architecture is happening by whether meaningful decisions are being made, made explicit, and helped to be understood; if not, it is not architecture.
Choose architecture consciously, because the default of no decision converges to a Big Ball of Mud and optimizing for local short-term change can inhibit global long-term change.
Make eliminating irreversibility one of the architect's most important tasks, because the best decision is often the one you do not need to make, achieved by building in options.
Run architecture reviews to examine the thinking — the decisions, assumptions, and principles — not only the artifact, and require every submitting team to provide an architecture decision record.

Take architecture seriously as an organization: do not stand up an architecture team only to routinely override it, since that pretends to define architecture and fails to attract or retain serious architects.

Treat good architecture as buying flexibility that pays off short-term and long-term — absorbing late requirements, avoiding lock-in, easing migration, enabling concurrent work — while accepting that architecture is trade-offs with rarely a single best answer weighed against context.

Test whether something is architecture by whether it contains nontrivial, context-driven decisions with their rationale, since architecture is the set of decisions that prevent needless creativity and cookie-cutter designs do not qualify.

Evaluate architecture as fit or unfit for a specific purpose and context rather than good or bad, making the assessment of context and hidden constraints a key architect responsibility, even accepting a Big Ball of Mud when only an immediate deadline matters.

Treat architecture as a combination of trade-offs across continua, and recognize that the self-inflicted 'no time for architecture' excuse produces a fragmented ad hoc landscape where temporary solutions last longest.
Treat software design and architecture as one continuum from high-level structure to low-level detail rather than two separate disciplines divided by a hard line.

Apply each programming paradigm for its architectural role — polymorphism to cross architectural boundaries, functional discipline to govern the location of and access to data, and structured programming as the algorithmic foundation of modules — understanding that each paradigm restricts rather than adds capability.
Apply restrictive, structured-programming-style disciplines and functional decomposition at the architectural level, defining modules, components, and services that are easily testable.

Treat components (the physical packaging of modules) as the fundamental building block and the lowest level an architect directly designs; leave class/function internals to developers and do not micromanage.

Never trade structure for short-term speed: making messes is always slower at every time scale and the cleanup-later promise never comes true, so the only way to go fast is to keep the code clean and well-structured.

Optimize end-to-end flow rather than individual steps, add the cost of delay to development cost, and beware that predictability optimization breeds sandbagging while avoiding duplication itself costs coordination — so some duplication can be the better speed trade-off.
Avoid the from-scratch rewrite as a fix for a messy system, because it is usually driven by the same overconfidence that produced the mess and tends to reproduce it.

Heed the hard-won structural lessons: code that nobody understands becomes officially rigid and worthless (clean code has real value), failing to isolate device and UI logic from business rules leaves a system unable to absorb a hardware change without a terrible hack, a from-scratch redesign team struggles to ever catch up with a staff actively extending the old system, forking a code base yields divergent versions that are hard to reintegrate, and failing to recognize an obvious boundary early costs a fortune later.

Keep software soft: design so the difficulty of a change is proportional only to the change's scope and not its shape, keeping the architecture as shape-agnostic as practical; disproportionate change cost is a signal that the system's shape conflicts with the requests.

Keep software soft by leaving as many options open as long as possible — the options being the details that do not matter — by decomposing every system into policy (the valuable business rules) and details (IO, database, web, frameworks, protocols) and shaping it so the policy is central and the details are irrelevant to it.
Design for change rather than fixed requirements, since requirements are always in flux, and recognize that evolvability is closely tied to a system's simplicity and the quality of its abstractions.

Reshape change-preventing controls such as budgeting, quality gates, and requirements documents to support change without discarding their original intent, because traditional IT wrongly treats 'no change' as the desired state.
Treat an architecture as a hypothesis to be proven by implementation and measurement rather than a frozen artifact, and remember that any diagram is only one chosen view, not the architecture itself.

Treat communication as critical to architect success and diagram with discipline: apply representational consistency, use low-fidelity ephemeral artifacts early to avoid Irrational Artifact Attachment, master tool features, follow conventions (solid=sync, dotted=async; UML for class/sequence; C4 for monoliths), and always include a key when shapes are ambiguous.

Treat architecture diagrams as purposeful models, not complete pictures: depict a scope meaningful, comprehensible, and cohesive, and only useful when it helps answer a specific question identified before drawing.

Reject architecture diagrams without connecting lines, because the lines carry relationships, coupling, and behavior — the same components wired differently yield opposite properties — and containment or proximity alone conveys no more than a bullet list.
Rely on the fact that the rules of architecture are largely the same across system types and stable over time, since they rest on the unchanging building blocks of sequence, selection, and iteration.
Keep architectures simple (KISS): independent components add complexity linearly while dependent ones add it exponentially, and complex systems only grow more complex when modified.
Govern macro structure such as layered-architecture access rules with fitness functions (for example ArchUnit or NetArchTest), not just diagrams.

Reason about systems with systems thinking that emphasizes behavior over structure, treating structure as only a means to achieve a desired behavior and recognizing systems architecture as a domain of organized complexity.

Treat object-oriented programming, to the architect, as the ability through safe polymorphism to gain absolute control over the direction of every source-code dependency; do not define OO by encapsulation or inheritance, which predate it and which OO did not strengthen.

Enforce architectural rules mechanically rather than by fallible discipline or slow post-compilation tooling: prefer to let the compiler enforce the architecture, applying access modifiers deliberately so only interfaces with inbound cross-package dependencies are public and implementation classes stay package-protected, because making all types public reduces packages to mere organization, collapses every architectural style to the same thing, and lets code instantiate concrete implementations directly in violation of the design.

Invert a dependency by interposing an interface so the source-code dependency points opposite to the flow of control, since without polymorphism source-code dependencies inexorably follow the flow of control.

Apply the Dependency Inversion Principle so source-code dependencies refer only to abstractions, reducing it to concrete rules — do not refer to, derive from, or override volatile concrete classes, and never name anything concrete and volatile — while tolerating stable concretions such as String and OS facilities, keeping interfaces stable by extending implementations, using an Abstract Factory to create volatile concretes, and using inheritance sparingly as the most rigid relationship.

Gather the unavoidable DIP violations into a small number of concrete components such as Main and keep them separate, recognizing that at a dependency-inversion boundary the source-code dependencies cross toward the abstract side while the flow of control crosses the other way — the basis of the Dependency Rule.

Distinguish the two boundary forms — dependency-normal, where source dependencies run with the flow of control yet still abstract the device, and dependency-inverted, where a higher-level component starts lower-level ones through a uniform polymorphic entry point so control flows opposite to dependencies — communicate across boundaries with short, simple, DSL-like command packets, and recall that routing inter-module calls through a runtime dispatch table makes modules independently deployable, which is polymorphism and a plugin architecture.

Arrange dependencies so the UI and the database depend on the business rules and become plugins to them, keeping business-rule source code free of any mention of the UI or database, which yields independent deployability and independent developability.

Point source-code dependencies toward the components you want to protect (make B depend on A to protect A), organizing components into a hierarchy of protection by level with the highest-level business rules the most protected, separating functionality by how, why, and when it changes and interposing interfaces to invert any policy-toward-detail dependency.

Put the database behind a data-access interface owned by the business rules so the database depends on the business rules and can be deferred or swapped, and treat both the database and the UI as irrelevant, replaceable plugins to the core model, with the less-relevant GUI depending on the business rules.
Design asymmetric plugin relationships that act as firewalls across which changes cannot propagate, so that the business rules do not break when a web page format or a database schema changes.

Identify the Critical Business Rules that make or save money even if executed manually, bind them with their Critical Business Data into Entities, and keep each Entity a pristine, self-standing business module usable in any system and unsullied by databases, UIs, or frameworks — requiring only that data and rules be bound in one separate module, not an object-oriented language.
Organize business logic so it can absorb change, because enterprise business rules are arbitrary, full of special cases, and certain to change over time.

Treat all concurrency hazards — races, deadlocks, and concurrent updates — as stemming from mutable state, and design for robustness under threads and processors by pushing as much processing as possible into immutable, purely functional components and driving code out of the components that must mutate.

Protect any necessary mutable state with transactional memory, and consider event sourcing — storing transactions and replaying them to derive state, with periodic snapshots to bound cost — to eliminate mutation and concurrent-update issues.

Recognize lost updates and inconsistent reads as the two essential concurrency failures, and treat concurrency control as a deliberate trade of correctness (safety) against liveness, calibrated to the likelihood and seriousness of the failures.

Design concurrency by creating isolated zones where programmers need not think about concurrency and pushing as much code as possible into them, leaning on isolation (only one agent touches a piece of data) and immutability (unchanging data needs no control); share immutable data widely and route read-only apps to copied data sources.

Avoid explicit multithreaded programming with locks and synchronization wherever possible, because it introduces defects that are almost impossible to reproduce; application developers should almost never handle explicit concurrency mechanisms.

Assume a node's execution can pause for a long time at any point (from stop-the-world garbage collection, virtual-machine suspension, swapping, or other causes) and be declared dead by others, so treat as unsafe any code that relies on synchronized clocks or assumes little time passes between checking a condition (such as lease validity) and acting on it, and remember that single-machine thread-safety tools like mutexes do not translate to a distributed system with no shared memory.

Use concurrency to improve performance where multiple CPUs or wait states exist, but manage shared state to prevent race conditions (via locks or per-thread state) and carefully identify critical sections, because race conditions are sporadic, timing-dependent, and among the hardest bugs to find.

Apply the Single Responsibility Principle so that a module is responsible to exactly one actor (not merely doing one thing): separate the code that different actors depend on, because co-locating it causes one actor's change to silently break another's behavior and invites risky merges, optionally separating data from functions behind a Facade.

Begin the initial architecture by identifying the actors and use cases, partition the system under the SRP so a change serving one actor does not affect another, separate components along the two dimensions of actor (SRP) and level of policy (Dependency Rule), and structure the build into fine-grained components for independent deliverables while reserving the right to regroup them, keeping using relationships pointing with the flow of control and inheritance relationships against it.
Ensure software entities do not depend on things they do not directly use, treating transitive dependencies as a violation.

Deliberately make some components unstable and have them depend on the stable ones (a system of all-stable components is unchangeable), and by convention draw unstable components at the top of a dependency diagram so any upward arrow visibly flags a Stable-Dependencies or Acyclic-Dependencies violation.

Enforce the Dependency Rule: source-code dependencies must point only inward toward higher-level policies, nothing in an inner circle may name anything declared in an outer circle, and outer-circle data formats (especially framework-generated ones) must not be used by an inner circle.
Guard against unnecessary brittleness: a failing external dependency should degrade gracefully rather than fail the whole system.
Never let the architecture depend on a particular version of a commercial product or tool; if such a dependency is unavoidable, isolate it so the version can be changed cheaply.

Apply the Interface Segregation Principle: do not depend on a module that carries more than you need, segregate fat interfaces into client-specific ones, and hide a component's internals so clients do not acquire transitive dependencies, because unneeded baggage forces needless recompilation and can propagate unexpected trouble.

Apply the Common Reuse Principle: do not force a component's users to depend on things they do not need, group classes that are reused together and depend heavily on each other, and keep only inseparable classes in one component since a user depends on the whole used component; this is the Interface Segregation Principle at component scale.

Use a Separated Interface to break a dependency that contradicts the general dependency structure by defining the interface in one package and implementing it in another (exploiting that an implementation depends on its interface but not the reverse, so other packages depend only on the interface), placing the interface in the client's package when there is a single client or all clients share a package, and in a third package when there are multiple clients or when the interface is not the client developers' responsibility.

Treat components as the units of deployment, keep well-designed components independently deployable and therefore independently developable, and decide which classes belong in which component by principle rather than ad hoc.

Support the whole lifecycle: make the system deployable in a single action and consider deployment from the start, mitigate maintenance cost (spelunking and the risk of inadvertent defects) by separating components behind stable interfaces, reveal operation by elevating use cases to first-class entities, and resist letting a development-schedule-driven structure such as one-component-per-team become the architecture.

Use the three structure categories for their intended reasoning: module structures for modifiability, component-and-connector structures for runtime qualities (performance, security, availability), and allocation structures for deployment-related qualities; no single structure is the architecture.

Adapt elements without changing them using interface tactics: tailor-interface to add or hide capabilities, configure-behavior to make components configurable at build/init/runtime, orchestrate to centralize coordination, and manage-resources via a resource manager that preserves invariants and reduces resource distance.

Do not design the component dependency structure top-down; let it evolve with the system as a map of buildability and maintainability rather than function, and shape it primarily to isolate volatility so that volatile components cannot affect stable, high-value components such as the business rules.

Apply the Stable Dependencies Principle: depend in the direction of stability so a volatile component is never depended on by one that is hard to change, measuring stability by the work required to change a component (its incoming dependencies) rather than its change frequency, and require the instability metric I = Fan-out/(Fan-in+Fan-out) to decrease along the direction of dependency.

Place high-level policy in stable components and volatile software in unstable ones, keeping the stable policy components abstract (interfaces and abstract classes) so per the OCP they stay extensible despite their stability — the Stable Abstractions Principle that a component should be as abstract as it is stable, which with the SDP forms the DIP for components so dependencies run toward abstraction.

Bind code to abstract device and service interfaces and keep high-level policy agnostic about physical and structural details (device independence, relative addressing), separating and decoupling policy from details so thoroughly that the policy has no knowledge of or dependency on them.
Keep architects writing code: a software architect is and remains a programmer and must keep experiencing the problems they create for the rest of the team.

Keep architects hands-on without becoming a bottleneck: never own critical-path/framework code; instead implement business functionality a few iterations downstream, or stay hands-on via POCs, tech-debt stories, bug fixes, tooling, and code reviews, writing POC code to production quality.
Keep architecture distinct from operations: do not let an architect become a perpetual firefighter, but still treat production issues as feedback on architectural weaknesses.
Keep EA tooling in service of the architects, since done poorly it becomes never-ending documentation that is outdated on publication.

Leave the operational and deployment mode open by keeping components isolated and free of assumptions about their communication mechanism, so the system can move among monolith, threads, processes, and services as operational needs change.

Recognize the three decoupling modes — source, deployment, and service — and, since the best mode is hard to know early and shifts as a project matures, leave the mode open: avoid defaulting to service-level decoupling (which is expensive and coarse) and instead push decoupling to the point where a service could be formed while keeping components in one address space as long as possible, protecting most source code from the change.

Adopt continuous deployment only where its value applies: just-in-time releases and fixes are a competitive or safety advantage, and it is undesirable or impossible for complex coordinated-release ecosystems and embedded, hard-to-access, or non-networked systems.

Partition the system into well-isolated, independently developable components that can be allocated to independent teams (Conway's law), make it immediately deployable after build, and use inexpensive partitioning principles to leave options open despite rarely knowing all use cases, constraints, and requirements up front.
Decouple architecture from development process, choosing top-level partitioning deliberately (technical vs domain) with full awareness of Conway's Law and the Inverse Conway Maneuver.

Use the SRP and CCP to separate things that change for different reasons into decoupled horizontal layers — UI, application-specific business rules, application-independent domain business rules, and the database — and additionally decouple use cases as thin vertical slices through those layers so new use cases can be added without disturbing existing ones.
Exploit that the decoupling done for use cases and layers also serves operations (separated components can run on and be replicated across servers) and supports any team organization.

Draw boundaries along an axis of change (the SRP tells you where) by partitioning the system into core-business-rule and plugin components and arranging all source-code arrows to point toward the core business, an application of the DIP and SAP with dependencies running from low-level details to high-level abstractions.

Distinguish true duplication (where every change to one instance forces the same change to the other) from accidental duplication (where similar sections change at different rates and will diverge), resist the knee-jerk unification of vertically separated use cases, and never pass a database record straight to the UI but introduce a separate view model.

Handle duplicates from retries via the end-to-end principle (deduplicate by a stable key at the end of each use case); better still, push exactly-once handling into the infrastructure rather than scattering deduplication logic through application code.

When the same data comes from multiple similar-but-different sources, interpose a two-step mapping (in-memory schema → logical store schema → physical schema) to cut duplication — but only when the sources share substantial commonality.

Manage boundary crossings by managing the source-code dependencies (a crossing is just a function call passing data), using dynamic polymorphism to invert the dependency against the flow of control so that all source-code dependencies cross toward the higher-level component, since component partitioning depends on such polymorphism.

Account for boundary-crossing cost when choosing a boundary: function calls within a monolith or deployment component are fast and tolerate chattiness, local-process crossings are moderately expensive, and service crossings over the network are slow and high-latency, so limit chattiness across stronger boundaries; treat threads as execution scheduling, not boundaries, and expect real systems to mix boundary types.

Cross boundaries against the flow of control with the DIP by having an inner-circle use case call an output-port interface that an outer-circle component implements, and let only simple, isolated data structures cross a boundary — never Entity objects or database rows — always in the form most convenient for the inner circle.

Treat deciding where architectural boundaries lie as a core function of the architect: boundaries appear along every axis of change (systems have more than the three obvious components), inter-component boundary APIs should be owned by the upstream higher-level component (the caller declares the interface the callee implements), and source-code dependencies should be directed by level toward the highest-level policy even when the data flow splits into several streams, with higher-level policy split from lower-level mechanics that declare events upward.

Model use cases as application-specific business rules that orchestrate the Entities, keep them free of any user-interface description so the delivery mechanism cannot be inferred from them, and make use cases depend on the more general Entities while the Entities never depend on the use cases.

Make the system's top-level structure scream its use cases and domain rather than its frameworks, centering the architecture on use cases so the supporting structures are described without committing to frameworks, databases, or web servers, because a framework-based architecture cannot be a use-case-based one.

Treat the web as a deferrable delivery-mechanism detail and keep the architecture as ignorant of delivery as possible, so the application could ship as a console, web, thick-client, or service application without fundamental change.

Use web services for application integration, not application construction: do not split one application into intercommunicating web services unless you really must; build the application and expose parts as Remote Facades, honoring the First Law of Distributed Object Design.
Treat a web service as fundamentally a remote interface plus a slow string-parsing step, so build the functionality fine-grained and layer a Remote Facade over it to expose web services.

View every framework skeptically, keep it at arm's length, and devise a strategy that prevents it from taking over the architecture, so that all use cases can be unit-tested without the web server, database, or frameworks — testability being an attribute of good architecture.
Continually analyze the live architecture (architecture vitality) to counter structural decay, and treat slow testing/release environments as agility risks.

Organize the architecture as concentric layers — Frameworks and Drivers, Interface Adapters, Use Cases, and Entities — with abstraction and policy increasing inward (the number of layers is not fixed but the Dependency Rule always holds), keep the Entities insulated from application-level operational changes, and confine all SQL and database knowledge to the interface-adapters layer so nothing inward of it knows the database.

Treat the database as a detail that must not pollute the architecture: distinguish the architecturally significant data model from the non-significant database, restrict knowledge of tabular structure to the outermost utility functions, never pass database rows or tables around as objects (which couples use cases, business rules, and the UI to the relational structure), encapsulate data-storage performance behind low-level access mechanisms, and when a non-engineering requirement forces a particular database, bolt it on the side behind a narrow, safe data-access channel while keeping the core data in the form most convenient to the application.

Avoid binding the business to volatile details and third parties: smearing embedded SQL and vendor APIs throughout the code traps you when the vendor product is cancelled (so isolate the database and avoid strong coupling to any third-party system), pointing dependencies along the flow of control instead of toward policy aids a product's demise (so direct dependencies toward policy), and a magical third-party database or framework can become a crippling dependency — while externalizing a state machine into a data file lets you change application flow, even at runtime, without changing code, an application of the OCP.

Use the layered (n-tier) architecture for small, simple, budget-constrained apps or as a temporary starting point, keeping closed layers of isolation, documenting which layers are open/closed and why, keeping reuse low and inheritance shallow, and watching for the architecture-sinkhole anti-pattern (apply the 80-20 rule).
Organize layered systems into closed layers with clear separation of concerns to enforce layers of isolation, keeping a change contained to its layer as long as the inter-layer contracts stay stable.

Use partial boundaries to reserve a place for a future full boundary when a full one is too expensive, choosing skip-the-last-step (build separable components but deploy them as one), a Strategy-based one-dimensional boundary, or a Facade, while accepting the YAGNI tension and that a partial boundary tends to degrade if the separation never materializes.

Balance the cost of boundaries deliberately: full boundaries are expensive but ignored ones are very expensive to retrofit even with tests and refactoring, so reconcile the YAGNI tension by guessing intelligently where boundaries lie and treat the decision as ongoing — watch the system and implement each boundary at the inflection point where implementing it costs less than continuing to ignore it.

Handle cross-cutting concerns — which afflict every system and especially break functionally decomposed services, where one feature can change them all — with an object and component design in which new features extend abstract base classes via Template Method or Strategy in new components that obey the Dependency Rule and load dynamically (OCP); design each service internally with the SOLID principles so the architectural boundaries run through services into components rather than between services.

Build layered architectures by programming to interfaces so service providers are substitutable, using header files as interface definitions limited to what callers need, limiting the visibility of implementation details and expecting them to change (the fewer places that know a detail, the fewer must change), and avoiding scattered conditional-compilation directives by hiding the target behind a HAL and binding through the linker or at runtime.

Group Service Layer operations into abstractions using vague heuristics: one abstraction for a small application, one per subsystem (vertical slice) for larger ones, or abstractions reflecting domain partitions or thematic behaviors.

Treat tests as a first-class part of the system that follow the Dependency Rule as the outermost circle (depending inward, with nothing depending on them), and never treat tests as outside the design, because poorly integrated tests become fragile and make the system rigid — the Fragile Tests Problem, where a trivial change breaks thousands of tests and developers then resist change.

Improve testability by limiting complexity and nondeterminism: avoid cyclic dependencies, isolate environmental dependencies, reduce coupling, simplify inheritance and keep response-of-a-class low, and remove avoidable sources of nondeterminism such as unconstrained parallelism, managing unavoidable nondeterminism with tactics like record/playback.

Apply testability-supporting patterns for their tradeoffs: dependency injection lets test instances replace production ones but reduces runtime predictability and adds up-front complexity, the strategy pattern allows runtime substitution of test versions but is wasted on simple classes, and intercepting filters add pre/post processing but can add latency.

Protect software's potential long life from unmanaged hardware and firmware dependencies: firmware is defined by what it depends on and how hard it is to change (burying SQL or spreading platform dependencies is writing firmware), and intermingling software and firmware is an anti-pattern, so separate business logic from hardware and platform and follow the order make it work, make it right, then make it fast.

Firm up the line between software and firmware with a Hardware Abstraction Layer whose API is tailored to the software's needs and hides how the hardware does its job, layering the system with the hardware at the bottom so an inevitable hardware change is not a bigger job than necessary, since the book's architectural principles apply to embedded systems and a clean embedded architecture eliminates the target-hardware test bottleneck.

Do not marry a framework: a framework is not an architecture and adopting one is an asymmetric marriage carrying real risk, so keep it at arm's length as an outer-circle detail and never let it into the inner circles, refuse to derive your business objects from its base classes (derive proxies in plugin components instead), use a framework such as Spring only in the Main component without scattering its annotations through business objects, and marry only the unavoidable frameworks such as the standard library, and only as a conscious decision.

Right-size the architecture and earn reuse: over-architecture with too many overhead-laden layers reduces productivity, so fit the architecture to the size of the problem rather than building enterprise-scale for a small tool, recognize that wildly different architectures (and service-oriented designs that are not clean plugin architectures) can each be effective, and never attempt a reusable framework before first making a usable one built in concert with several reusing applications.

Choose a code organization that screams the domain and enforces dependency direction: package-by-layer is a quick start that does not scream the domain and does not scale, package-by-feature screams the domain but is still suboptimal, so prefer ports-and-adapters where the outside depends on the inside and never the reverse, name inside elements in the ubiquitous domain language, and beware that a strict layered graph can be cheated into a relaxed layered architecture in which a controller bypasses the service layer to call a repository directly and skips logic such as authorization.

Use package-by-component to bundle a coarse-grained component's business logic and persistence behind one clean interface (keeping the UI separate) as a stepping stone toward micro-services, and decouple further with module systems that distinguish public from published types or with separate source trees where the outside depends only on the domain — while guarding against the Périphérique anti-pattern in which all infrastructure in one source tree lets one area call another without passing through the domain.

Remember that the implementation strategy can destroy good design intentions, so map the design onto concrete code structures, choose decoupling modes pragmatically for the team's size, skill, and budget, use the compiler to enforce the style, and watch for coupling in other areas such as data models.

Make architecture analysis systematic with tactics, which fill gaps a pattern leaves, let you build a design fragment from first principles when no pattern exists, and must be refined into a concrete context-appropriate strategy when applied.
Do not share a database across services; share data through an event log and well-defined service interfaces, and hide internal data, so services can evolve their schemas and code independently.

Treat reuse as double-edged: avoid sharing databases or a single domain model across services, and recognise that clean encapsulation breaks down once requirements crosscut service boundaries and force several services to change together.

Recognise the data dichotomy — databases expose data while services hide it — and that core data coupling is unavoidable; manage it deliberately to avoid the God Service, REST-to-ETL polling, and proliferating mutable copies that drive data divergence.

Treat the organization as an unbundled database turned inside out: a single shared log feeds many independently tunable views (a database of databases), giving more malleability than one shared database while keeping applications loosely coupled and query functionality private to each service.
Prefer asynchronous event / publish-subscribe integration over a growing web of synchronous request-response calls, to limit cascading failures and keep the system pluggable.
Use asynchronous messaging for reliable, decoupled, retryable communication via store-and-forward and automatic retry, accepting the added event-driven design complexity as a deliberate trade-off.

Use an Event Message for reliable asynchronous notification — broadcast on a Publish-Subscribe Channel with often non-durable subscribers, kept timely with Message Expiration rather than Guaranteed Delivery — and choose between push and pull notification based on how many observers want the details.
Use a Durable Subscriber when an observer must not miss notifications published while it is temporarily disconnected.
Implement the Observer pattern across distributed applications with a Publish-Subscribe Channel, letting the subject announce a change with one message that the channel copies to every subscriber.

Keep concurrent asynchronous flows separate with a unique Correlation Identifier propagated through every request and reply and filtered by a Selective Consumer, registering listening subjects up front so a reply cannot arrive before the process is listening, and use publish-subscribe to ease whole-flow monitoring.

Use a replayable, retentive log (e.g. Kafka) as the shared source of truth — a middle ground between ephemeral messaging and a queryable database — so services stay decoupled yet have a durable store to fall back to and replay from.

Build read views (materialized views, polyglot views, MemoryImages) from the log, each tuned to a use case and independently scalable, choosing the right tool (Kafka Streams, KSQL, Connect single-message transforms) and storage technology for the query shape.

Use a Message Store, populated asynchronously via a Wire Tap in fire-and-forget mode, to capture message data centrally for reporting, balancing stored detail against traffic and storage, choosing a per-type or generic-XML schema by reporting needs, purging growth, and combining wire taps to analyze relationships between messages.
Treat streaming as a change in mindset: model the business as continuous streams of facts and services as functions that transform them, rather than as request/response over a database.

Keep stream-processing state local rather than pushing it into a remote database, treating it as a declaratively defined, continuously updated cache, for faster processing and greater service autonomy.

Match the stream-processing use to its pattern: complex event processing and stream search store queries long-term and let data flow past them (reversing the usual database roles), stream analytics computes windowed aggregations and may use probabilistic algorithms as an optimization without being inherently lossy, and maintaining materialized views from a change stream needs all events back to the beginning rather than just a recent window.
Make stateful stream processing keep its state local and back it to Kafka so computations survive crash/restart; avoid a per-event network call on a high-throughput stream.
Make stateful stream processing operationally practical with standby replicas, periodic disk checkpoints, and compacted topics to bound cold-start and rebuild times.
Use Kafka transactions to write atomically across multiple topics and to tie a state-store write to its output message, so partial failures cannot leave the system in an inconsistent state.

Understand Kafka exactly-once as broker idempotence plus an atomic commit that ties output messages and consumer-offset commits together; it covers only the Kafka parts of the system and, with the Kafka Streams API, is enabled rather than hand-coded.

Build stream processing with Kafka Streams (JVM DSL blended with functional per-message operators) or KSQL for non-JVM use to model business operations asynchronously and coordination-free, and route reads across instances with the metadata service when exposing state stores over HTTP.

For correct concurrent state mutation, wrap the critical section in a Kafka transaction and partition the work by the relevant business key; otherwise a failure leaves the system in an unknown state and parallel instances bottleneck on a shared database.
Use Kafka Streams state stores — local, disk-resident, Kafka-backed key/value stores that participate in transactions and are restored on restart — as the durable local state for stream processing.
Centralize an immutable stream of facts but decentralize the freedom to act; avoid an ESB-style central team that dictates schemas, flows, validation, and transformation.

Prefer choreography (Event Collaboration, no central owner of the workflow) for large workflows that span teams and change independently, and orchestration when central control and single-place reasoning matter more.

Partition by a business key to guarantee per-key ordering, since ordering holds only within a partition; use a single-partition topic only when global ordering is required, accepting single-machine throughput.
Ensure strong ordering guarantees for business state updates by routing related messages to the same partition via a key; accept relaxed ordering only for analytics-style workloads.
Keep partitioning keys invariant across all messages for an entity to preserve ordering, enforcing this at the domain level (for example, requiring a new order when the product changes).

Partition (shard) data when a single machine cannot hold the dataset or sustain the query throughput, usually combining partitioning with replication, and design the partitioning to spread data and load evenly to avoid skew and hot spots, noting that purely random assignment avoids hot spots but makes it impossible to find a record without querying every node.

Treat routing a request to the partition holding a key as a service-discovery problem solved by contacting any node that forwards, a partition-aware routing tier, or partition-aware clients, and propagate the authoritative partition-to-node map through a coordination service like ZooKeeper or a gossip protocol so all participants agree.

Recognize that a total order alone is insufficient for problems like a uniqueness constraint because the order only emerges after all operations are collected, so you also need to know when it is finalized, which is what total order broadcast provides through its reliable-delivery and totally-ordered-delivery safety properties; note that single-leader-per-partition databases maintain ordering only within a partition and so need extra coordination for cross-partition guarantees.
Get durability and throughput from replication plus producer retries; enable retries for transient failures and constrain in-flight batches per destination so retried batches cannot reorder events.

Choose a replication-log method by its trade-offs: statement-based replication breaks on nondeterministic or order-dependent statements, write-ahead-log shipping ties replication to the storage format and blocks zero-downtime upgrades, trigger-based replication is flexible but costly and bug-prone, so prefer a decoupled logical (row-based) log that stays compatible across versions and underlies change data capture.

Exploit the log-structured design (append-only, sequential IO, zero-copy, O(1) partition reads/writes) for cheap retention and high throughput, and size clusters knowing replication overhead roughly divides ingest throughput by three.

Use a log-based message broker, which combines database durability with low-latency notification by appending to a partitioned append-only log with per-message offsets, supports fan-out (multiple consumers read independently) and load-balances by assigning whole partitions (so parallelism is capped at the partition count and a slow message blocks its partition), and tracks progress cheaply by periodically recording each consumer's offset.

For sensitive datasets configure three replicas per partition, make the producer wait for replication before proceeding, and enable retries; use synchronous disk flush only sparingly because it sharply reduces throughput.

Ensure every replication scheme converges so all replicas reach the same final value, choosing a convergent conflict-resolution method consciously: last-write-wins and highest-replica-id both lose data, merging values or recording the conflict for later resolution preserve more, so avoid last-write-wins when data loss is unacceptable.

Achieve exactly-once correctness across partitions without an atomic commit by first durably logging the request as a single atomically-written message and then deriving the per-partition instructions from it with a deterministic processor that carries the request ID, so downstream processors deduplicate by that ID even after a crash reprocesses the request.

Break synchronous coupling between independently operated services using asynchronicity and a broker, and lean on receiver-driven routing so receivers control their participation and the system stays pluggable.

Accept that loose coupling adds complexity and use message-oriented middleware to supply the common formats, queuing channels, and transformers that make loosely coupled exchange nearly as easy as a direct call.
Use a Message Broker to centralize routing so applications need not know one another, enabling non-intrusive integration of packaged and legacy systems as the integration equivalent of a Mediator.

Because popular web-service protocols are stateless and unreliable, build an explicit transaction or compensation scheme so a set of asynchronous service invocations can fail or roll back atomically, leveraging coordination-context standards or reliable-messaging frameworks like ebMS where available.

Use asynchronous message passing through a broker to gain buffering when a recipient is unavailable, automatic redelivery, sender-recipient decoupling, and one-to-many fan-out; since brokers do not enforce a data model, use a backward- and forward-compatible encoding so publishers and consumers can be changed and deployed independently.

Choose between event notification and event-carried state transfer by architecture size: emphasise notification for small/lightweight systems and replication for large systems that need service autonomy; blend both within bounded contexts.

Use event-driven architecture for distributed asynchronous, decoupled event processing, choosing the broker topology for high responsiveness/scale with simple flows and the mediator topology when you need workflow control, error handling, recoverability, and restart.
Choose event-driven architecture for highly scalable, adaptable applications built from decoupled, single-purpose components that asynchronously receive and process events.
Communicate between independently deployable microservices with asynchronous message passing while keeping each service's internal logic synchronous.

Build microservices as the physical embodiment of bounded context with strict data isolation (no shared schemas/databases as integration points), letting each team pick its own data store and accepting performance overhead from network calls and per-endpoint security.

Choose microservices — a distributed architecture of separately deployed service components accessed via remote protocols — when you need robustness, independent scalability, and continuous delivery; it evolved specifically to simplify monolith and SOA pain.

Reduce microservices coupling by serving one component's cross-component data needs from a shared database instead of invoking another service component, and by copying small shared functionality across components (accepting a deliberate DRY trade-off) to preserve independence and separate deployment.

Plan for the distributed costs of microservices: real-time per-component deployments enable continuous availability, but you inherit event-driven architecture's contract governance, remote availability, and remote authentication/authorization problems.

Compose stream operators into a dataflow system for the microservices benefit of loose coupling and independent deployment but with one-directional asynchronous streams, and for a dependency such as an exchange rate prefer subscribing to a stream of updates and querying a local copy over a synchronous per-request call to a remote service, which is faster and more robust because the fastest, most reliable network request is no network request at all.

Use Event Sourcing — append each state change as a new immutable event instead of updating in place — to gain a complete audit log, the ability to rederive current state, and simple recover-by-replay, with little extra recovery code.

Treat mutable state and an append-only log of immutable events as two sides of the same coin and the log as the source of truth from which state is derived, gaining accounting-ledger-style auditability (correcting mistakes with compensating events rather than erasing) and capturing more information than the current state alone, such as a cart item that was added and later removed.

Adopt a trust-but-verify culture of continually auditing a system's own integrity rather than assuming correctness guarantees are absolute, favor event-based designs that are more auditable because their deterministic derivations can be re-run and their logs hash-checked, and perform integrity checks end to end so that every disk, network, service, and algorithm along a derived-data pipeline is implicitly covered.

Apply CQRS — separate the read path from the write path through an asynchronous channel — so each can be optimized independently; accept that the read model lags the write model and add a strategy for read-your-writes when needed.
Collapse CQRS asynchrony for clients that must read their own writes by blocking the read (long polling with nonblocking IO) until the awaited event arrives in the view or a timeout passes.

Make the event stream the single source of truth and derive every read model or view from it, eliminating the dual-write atomicity problem and the divergence between a service's internal state and the state it communicates.

Understand event-driven architecture's profile: technically partitioned with quanta joined by shared databases or request-reply, rating very high on performance, scalability, and fault tolerance but low on simplicity and testability due to nondeterministic flows.

Plan for event-driven architecture's asynchronous-distributed complexity up front (remote availability, responsiveness, broker/mediator reconnection), and treat the lack of atomic transactions as a disqualifier when a single undivided transaction must span event processors.

Account for the main downside of event sourcing and change data capture, that asynchronous consumers can leave a user reading a log-derived view that does not yet reflect their own write, while exploiting that deriving state from a log simplifies concurrency control, since a self-contained event is a single atomic append and a single-threaded consumer of a partition that matches the state's partitioning needs no write concurrency control.

Achieve exactly-once (effectively-once) semantics so the visible output is as if each record were processed once, using microbatching or checkpointing for fault tolerance within the framework, but recognizing that those do not cover external side effects, so make all of an event's outputs and side effects take effect atomically only if processing succeeds.

Design for change at company scale by treating it as a people problem as much as a software one: breaking a monolith alone does not improve sustainability — manage organization, software, and data together as they evolve.

Change organizational structure, processes, and culture alongside technology, since DevOps needs broken run-and-change silos, cloud needs empowered developers, and analytics needs hard-data decisions, which has broadened the architect's role to designing the organization and culture and rewards hands-on change agents over ivory-tower diagrammers.

Favour immutable, deterministically rederivable views over long-lived mutated databases, and recreate views from the log when moving between environments instead of copying database files or relying on rarely-used data scripts.

Separate the immutable event log from mutable state so you can derive several read-optimized views from the same log (command query responsibility segregation), which eases evolution because a new view can be built alongside existing systems and the old one retired later instead of doing a complex in-place migration.
Model identity to correlate with the real world, give logically mutable entities a version identifier, and use optimistic concurrency control (server-side version comparison) to reject stale writes.

Evolve schemas additively for backward/forward compatibility, enforce compatibility with a schema registry that fails incompatible messages on publication, and use schema-on-read so multiple versions can coexist.

Use Unit of Work to track every object read and modified and orchestrate all writes in a single commit, concentrating commit sequencing and key dependencies in one place; it becomes essential once database interactions grow awkward.

Implement pessimistic locks with shared/exclusive read-write locks (many readers, one writer excludes all) and optimistic locks with a version marker (timestamp or counter) compared on update for lost updates and on every datum read for inconsistent reads.

Use a Unit of Work to track every object created, updated, and deleted (and optionally read, to detect inconsistent reads) during a business transaction, then on commit open a transaction, perform concurrency checking, and write the changes, so programmers never explicitly call update methods or worry about referential-integrity ordering.

Implement a Coarse-Grained Lock by sharing one version object across a group of related objects, ensuring all of them reference the exact same version instance by caching versions in a session-scoped Identity Map.

Manage a shared (Coarse-Grained Lock) version's persistence deliberately: separate its database insert from its creation so insertion defers until at least one owner is inserted (tracking whether it is new so it inserts only once), increment it once per change set after first checking it is not already locked and then verifying a non-zero affected row count (zero signals a concurrency violation), and increment only in the system transaction that commits, using a separate checkCurrent method to verify currency in an earlier transaction without updating.

Detect concurrency with per-key version numbers (requiring a client to read before writing and to merge the values it read), have clients merge concurrent siblings rather than relying on lossy last-write-wins, use a tombstone deletion marker so a union merge does not resurrect removed items, and prefer conflict-free replicated datatypes that merge automatically and preserve deletions because hand-written sibling merges are error-prone.

Use multi-object transactions to coordinate writes that must stay in sync (foreign-key references, denormalized values, and secondary indexes), grouping the operations by some boundary such as the client's TCP connection in relational databases, and recognize that many nonrelational stores lack such grouping so a multi-key operation can partially succeed.

Rely on the near-universal single-object atomicity and isolation that storage engines provide (a crash-recovery log for atomicity and a per-object lock for isolation), and use single-object atomic operations like increment and compare-and-set to avoid read-modify-write races, while remembering these are not transactions in the sense of grouping multiple objects.

Use snapshot isolation, in which each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of data committed at its start, for read skew that read committed permits and that is intolerable for backups and long analytic queries; it is implemented with multi-version concurrency control where reads take no locks (readers never block writers) and transaction-ID visibility rules present each transaction a consistent point-in-time view.

Where available, rely on automatic lost-update detection because it needs no special application code and is less error-prone than locks, use compare-and-set only after verifying it is not unsafe against a stale snapshot, and remember that locks and compare-and-set assume a single up-to-date copy and so do not apply to multi-leader or leaderless replication, which instead rely on merging siblings and commutative operations.

Compose diverse storage and processing tools in two complementary ways, a federated database that unifies reads behind one query interface and an unbundled database that unifies writes by plugging systems together with change data capture and event logs, and to synchronize writes across heterogeneous systems prefer an asynchronous ordered event log with idempotent writes over distributed transactions, which lack a standard cross-technology protocol.

Preserve integrity in a dataflow system without distributed transactions by combining four mechanisms: representing each write as a single atomically-written message (fitting event sourcing), deriving all other state with deterministic functions, passing a client-generated request ID through every stage for end-to-end duplicate suppression, and keeping messages immutable and reprocessable to recover from bugs.

Because no single tool serves all use cases, compose several systems by letting data flow between them through batch processing and event streams with designated systems of record and derived data, make those derivations asynchronous and loosely coupled so a fault in one area does not spread and the system is easier to evolve, and implement strong integrity scalably with end-to-end operation identifiers for idempotence and asynchronous constraint checking, which is more robust than distributed transactions.

For non-backward-compatible schema changes use the Dual Schema Upgrade Window with v1 and v2 topics; choose the up-convert or internal-migrate variant when historic messages must be back-populated, and note that a single writer makes such upgrades far simpler.

Handle a data-format change according to the schema approach: with schema-on-read, write new documents carrying the new fields and handle old documents in application code; with schema-on-write, run a migration; and prefer schema-on-read when the data is heterogeneous (many object types, or a structure controlled by external systems that may change).

Treat schemas as version-controlled code and collaborate on changes through pull requests, which reach and audit consensus without impeding the implementer, rather than via ad hoc email or a central gatekeeping team.

Treat document databases as having an implicit schema rather than being schemaless, and distinguish schema-on-read (structure interpreted at read, like dynamic typing) from schema-on-write (explicit and enforced, like static typing), recognizing that whether to enforce schemas is a contentious choice with no universally right answer.
Plan for messages that are valid by schema but unreadable or semantically invalid: route them to a separate error topic so processing continues and the errors can be reprocessed later.

Handle problem messages distinctly: route messages a receiver cannot process to an Invalid Message Channel and rely on the system's Dead Letter Channel for undeliverable messages, designing custom invalid-message handling since dead-message handling is fixed by the platform.

Scale stateful operations by partitioning (rekeying / co-partitioning) on a business key so each key is processed single-threaded and atomically with no cross-network coordination — like the Map phase of MapReduce — and chain stages that need different distributions via rekey operations.
Use the AKF Scale Cube as the framework for scaling: clone (X) for transactions, split different things (Y) by function/resource, split similar things (Z) by customer.

Treat MapReduce as a low-level model between declarative and imperative whose map and reduce functions must be pure, and prefer a declarative aggregation interface when available, since two carefully coordinated functions are harder to write than one query and give the optimizer fewer opportunities.

Plan rebalancing to leave load fairly shared, keep serving reads and writes throughout, and move no more data than necessary; never assign keys with hash mod N (which moves most keys when the node count changes), and instead use a fixed large number of partitions, dynamic split-and-merge partitioning, or a fixed number of partitions per node.

Scale serial execution beyond a single CPU core only by partitioning so each transaction touches a single partition (cross-partition transactions are vastly slower), and respect its constraints: every transaction must be small and fast because one slow transaction stalls all, the active dataset must fit in memory, and write throughput must fit one core or be partitioned without cross-partition coordination.

Use the MapReduce model of four steps (split into records, a stateless mapper extracting key-value pairs, an implicit sort by key, and a reducer over each key's values) to parallelize a computation across machines without writing parallelism code, since the framework partitions the work and tries to run each mapper on a machine that already holds a replica of its input.

Scale organizations with systems-design techniques — statelessness, horizontal scaling, minimal sync points, local transaction scope, async over synchronous, caching — since in a massively scaling world humans and organizations become the limit, and improve personal throughput by minimizing open tasks.
Minimize the assumptions and dependencies between integrated systems (loose coupling) so each can change, fail, or run independently without cascading change across the others.

Preserve loose coupling by sending Event Messages and letting other systems decide what to do, rather than baking downstream requirements into the source, which would shift an event toward a command and tightly couple the systems.
Do not introduce messaging when remote cross-process communication is not actually required; use the simplest in-process mechanism such as shared memory or concurrent collections.

Coordinate a message with a database or workflow inside a transaction — consume, act, then commit, or act then send then commit — using a distributed transaction because each resource has its own transaction manager, so no message is lost and no required message is forgotten.

Expose a set of collaborating services as a business process component with a single endpoint that manages internal message flow and inter-service dependencies, so clients need not implement their own Process Manager, and have a process container implement the Message Translator, Service Activator, and Envelope Wrapper patterns.

Treat remote calls as never performance-transparent: an in-process call is fast, an interprocess call is orders of magnitude slower, and a cross-machine call another order or two slower again, so distributing objects has more pitfalls than commonly realized.
Exploit asynchrony deliberately for throttling, load balancing, variable-pace producer/consumer throughput, disconnected operation, and callback-based thread management.
Favor asynchronous communication to decouple services and prevent cascading failure; make external, long-running, error-prone, or unconstrained calls async, and give synchronous calls timeouts.
Bridge synchronous and asynchronous styles with Request-Reply when an interactive, immediate response is required.

Choose how a requestor receives a reply: a Synchronous Block via a Polling Consumer is simple but recovers poorly from crashes and implies one outstanding request, while an Asynchronous Callback supports many outstanding requests on one reply channel and easy recovery at the cost of callback-context complexity.

Prefer asynchronous, queue-based communication that backs off rather than piling on retries, but manage its read cost, and answer questions where everyone can search the reply to load a cache instead of repeating yourself.
Treat message ordering as something you must re-establish explicitly, because channels guarantee delivery but not timing and async results can complete in any order.
Send a message on a Point-to-Point Channel whenever it must be consumed by exactly one receiver.
Prefer ETL tools over messaging for large one-time bulk data movement, and use messaging to keep systems in sync after the initial replication.

Decide between carrying reference data in each transaction message and replicating it separately based on its change frequency and the coupling cost; propagate low-frequency changes via a dedicated Publish-Subscribe Channel.

Use messaging to transfer data frequently, immediately, reliably, and asynchronously with retry and in-transit transformation, while accepting its learning curve, harder testing, glue-code burden, and residual update lag.

Use broadcasting for maximum decoupling (and eventual-consistency/CEP patterns), and implement EDA synchronous needs with request-reply messaging, preferring a correlation ID over per-request temporary queues at volume.

Manage replicated-cache data collisions by modeling the collision rate (rises with instances, update rate, and replication latency; falls with cache size) and reducing latency or instance count when needed.
Match replication mechanism to dataset: snapshot small tables (use flipping snapshots to avoid blocking reads) and use the database's bulk-load facility for bulk movement.
Describe and compare integration designs in a vendor-neutral pattern vocabulary rather than product-specific jargon, to enable confident decisions across heterogeneous middleware.

Adhere to standards as a primary enabler of integrability and interoperability, but only credit the dimensions a standard actually addresses and the likelihood that future suppliers conform; abstract common services behind a shared abstraction so future components integrate once and cross-cutting concerns change in fewer places.
Do not assume different messaging systems interconnect or that any capability such as publish-subscribe is universally available; verify per product and plan bridging where needed.
Route messages through a broker or router rather than making each sender know and target every recipient, because sender-side recipient knowledge does not scale and breaks whenever a system is added.

To deliver to interested and authorized recipients with tight control, use a Dynamic Recipient List rather than open broadcast, given that publish-subscribe lets any subscriber listen and duplicates traffic over wide-area networks.

Choose the channel kind by delivery intent: a Point-to-Point Channel for exactly-once consumption (scaled by Competing Consumers, with Request-Reply over channel pairs for messaging RPC) and a Publish-Subscribe Channel to deliver a copy to every interested receiver, as Event Messages typically require.
Use a publish-to-a-group messaging bus to decouple clients from servers so a client sends one message and the bus fans it out reliably to all participants.

Connect applications that were not built for messaging through an explicit endpoint or channel-adapter layer, and insert translators wherever producer and consumer formats, identifiers, or encodings disagree.

Deliberately remove the four coupling assumptions — platform representation, location, time, and data format — using self-describing platform-independent formats, addressable channels, request queuing, and in-channel transformation.
Connect non-messaging applications through explicit message endpoints or Channel Adapters, and isolate application code from messaging-specific code behind a Messaging Gateway.

Prefer dedicated, consistent Message Translators over transformation logic hand-coded inside a gateway or process manager, which insulates downstream logic from source-format changes and avoids error-prone duplication.

Apply transformation at the correct layer (transport, data representation, data types, data structures) and chain one Message Translator per layer with Pipes and Filters for reuse and interchangeability, since channels and routers leave applications coupled by format until a translator removes that dependency.

Connect applications through Channel Adapters at the appropriate layer — preferring a stable business-logic API over brittle screen-scraping or risky direct database writes — and combine each adapter with a Message Translator to produce Canonical Data Model messages.

When deploying Channel Adapters remotely over HTTP or ODBC, account for the loss of messaging quality of service, use Metadata adapters to extract format information, and implement adapters as Transactional Clients so work succeeds in both systems.

Adopt a Canonical Data Model to avoid the N-square translator explosion: with each application translating only to and from the common format, the translator count grows linearly, adding a new application needs only one translator pair, and a Message Broker should use a CDM internally.
Design widely distributed solutions for network reality — slow and unreliable links and heterogeneous platforms — rather than as if they were a single in-process application.
