Design distributed systems against the eight fallacies of distributed computing: the network is unreliable (use timeouts/circuit breakers), latency is non-zero (track average and tail latency), bandwidth is finite (minimize data, avoid stamp coupling), the network is insecure (secure every endpoint), the topology changes (stay close to ops), there are many administrators, transport costs money, and the network is heterogeneous.
Never treat a common data representation as common semantics; explicitly resolve semantic differences between systems as a combined business and technical task.

Expect semantic and conceptual dissonance when integrating heterogeneous systems, where the same data field means different things across divisions, and plan reconciliation rather than assuming shared meaning.

Never portray remote communication as a local method call; design explicitly for remote-call realities of latency, failure, security, and changing signatures, since the local-call abstraction yields brittle, unscalable systems.

Recognize that Remote Procedure Invocation applies useful encapsulation but still leaves applications tightly coupled and sequencing-bound, and that its local-call familiarity is a trap because remote calls differ greatly in performance and reliability.
Minimize remote calls, because latency typically dominates the cost of distributed systems and is something the application developer can do little to improve.

Do not try to make a remote service look like a local object, because the RPC ideal of location transparency is fundamentally flawed: a network request can be lost, time out leaving the outcome unknown, be silently duplicated by retries, have wildly variable latency, and cross language boundaries, which is why newer RPC frameworks are explicit about a remote call being different (using futures and streams).
Perform data-format translation outside the applications, because an application's internal format usually cannot be changed to suit others.
Adopt a Canonical Data Model and convert each application's format to it via translators, keeping public canonical messages separate from private application-specific messages.
Build a systems-management function into the solution from the start to monitor data flow, verify component availability, and report errors centrally.

Operate and verify a running solution actively: collect metrics through a Control Bus and periodically inject Test Messages whose results are checked by a Test Data Verifier, plus statistical sampling to catch validly-formatted but wrong data.

Automate failover by having a management console subscribe to component status events from the Control Bus and a failover handler send a command to a Context-Based Router that re-routes requests from a failed primary to a standby secondary.

Give each channel a single message type (Datatype Channel) and a naming convention that reinforces the public/private split, so consumers know what to expect and application-specific messages stay private.

Design notification channels to deliver only what observers need without channel explosion: keep one message type per channel, group similar notifications going to the same audience onto a shared channel, separate unrelated audiences, and use Selective Consumers rather than forcing observers to monitor many channels.

Do not use Selective Consumers to hide messages from other consumers, since selection criteria are not authorized — use separate Datatype Channels for security — and use a Message Dispatcher to centralize selection, handle unmatched messages, and implement a default case.

Choose channel type by communication direction and audience: use Point-to-Point for client-to-server and Publish-Subscribe for server-to-client, broadcast on per-user channels so all of a multi-login user's clients get the message, avoid blanket broadcast at high volume, and place consolidation logic to avoid duplicating channels across messaging systems.

Design every Aggregator around three explicit decisions — correlation, completeness condition, and aggregation algorithm — and correlate by a unique per-transaction identifier rather than a shared attribute.

Design an Aggregator around correlation, a completeness condition, and an aggregation strategy, keeping the aggregation logic in strongly-typed domain objects independent of the messaging API and using a channel abstraction so the same code runs over queues in production and topics for debugging.
For an immediate, always-current synchronous read, accessing the data directly as a Shared Database is the simplest efficient option, accepting the resulting tight coupling to the schema.

Use a Shared Database for strong consistency only with eyes open: a unified schema is technically hard and politically contentious, often impossible for packaged apps, prone to lock contention and bottlenecks, and unable to trigger cross-application processes.

Consider representing reads as events routed through the same stream operator as writes (a stream-table join between read queries and the database, which also aids provenance tracking), and treat queries as streams to enable distributed execution of complex queries that combine data across several partitions, reusing the message-routing and join infrastructure.
Make services reusable by exposing an interface contract and supporting a Return Address, and wrap legacy services that lack these features in a Smart Proxy that also tracks quality of service.

Insert a Smart Proxy to track request-reply services and collect operational metrics — restoring the consumer's Return Address and Correlation Identifier — reporting metrics to the Control Bus on a timer using snapshots and thread-safe collections because consumer threads update the data concurrently.
Use Message Filters so each system receives only the messages matching its criteria.
Use a Message Filter to drop unwanted messages from a channel based on criteria, running it stateless for parallelism or stateful when it must remember history such as for de-duplication.

Prefer coarse-grained, self-contained business actions over fine-grained interfaces, because fine-grained interfaces cause excessive remote calls, synchronization overhead, and tight coupling — while balancing against interfaces so coarse they limit flexibility.
Give a distributed object a coarse-grained remote interface (fewer, bulkier calls to minimize round trips) distinct from its fine-grained local interface, accepting a more awkward programming model.
Design integration by the rules of crossing application boundaries, not the rules of a single application, and use asynchronous thinking to push toward high local cohesion and low remote coupling.
Recognize that classic code-level coupling metrics miss the architect-level question of synchronous versus asynchronous communication in distributed systems.

Construct messages deliberately: package data into messages, choose the message type by intent (command, document, event, request-reply), split oversized data into a Message Sequence, set a Message Expiration when data is time-limited, and agree the format via a Canonical Data Model.
Split data too large for one message into a Message Sequence so the receiver can reassemble it, and set a Message Expiration on data that becomes useless after a deadline.

Handle large data as a Message Sequence robustly: mark each part with sequence, position, and size-or-end fields, send even single messages as sequences when the receiver expects them, transmit on a single-consumer channel inside a Transactional Client, reroute incomplete sequences to the Invalid Message Channel, and use a Claim Check when both sides share a datastore.

Manage leftover and stuck messages: use a Correlation Identifier to detect a stale reply, remember that transactions do not fix programming errors that strand messages, and use a Channel Purger to clear all or selected messages (storing them for inspection or replay), with temporary channels or removing a poison message to restore a crashing recipient.

Throttle an overwhelming message flow with a Message Filter that drops messages arriving within a small time window of the last accepted one, which is acceptable when frequent updates make occasional data loss tolerable.

Plan channels deliberately: they are created through administration tools and fixed at deployment, so dedicate one message type per channel, provide an Invalid Message Channel, and recognize that a well-designed channel set forms a Message Bus.

Treat channels as cheap but not free — each consumes memory and persistent channels consume disk — and choose and test a highly scalable messaging implementation if the design may need very large numbers of channels.

Use asynchronous pipelines to raise throughput, parallelize the slowest stage with Competing Consumers on a Point-to-Point Channel, parallelize only stateless filters, and preserve ordering with a single instance or a Resequencer when sequence is critical.

Draw design guidance from the mostly asynchronous real world: optimize for throughput with queues that decouple producer and consumer, scale with competing consumers, and carry a correlation identifier to match out-of-order results.
Make production filters transactional so a failure before the output is sent does not lose the message.

Make a filter transactional as a Send-Receive Message Pair by opening a transaction before consuming the input and committing after publishing the output, aborting on any exception to roll back both and return the input to the queue.

Do not solve content routing by creating a channel per message type or by letting consumers self-select after consuming, because these cause channel explosion and tie components to message types; use a Message Router instead.

Use a Message Router to keep destination decisions in a single location — adding types or rules then changes only the router and routing all messages through it preserves order — without modifying message content.
Use a Content-Based Router so producers send to a single channel and the router directs each message to its proper destination, avoiding coupling the producer to specific destination channels.

Do not achieve fine-grained routing through channel subscription alone or by broadcasting and filtering inside each component, because binary subscription causes channel explosion, originator-maintained recipient preferences become a maintenance nightmare, and in-component filtering assumes control over apps you usually lack.

Weigh a Message Router's downsides: it must know every destination and becomes a maintenance bottleneck and added-latency step, so when the destination set changes frequently prefer reactive filtering with a Publish-Subscribe Channel and Message Filters.

Choose between predictive routing (a Content-Based Router) and reactive filtering (a Publish-Subscribe Channel with Message Filters) by who should control routing, whether multiple recipients must process a message, network topology, and data sensitivity — routers suit business transactions and sensitive data, filter arrays suit event notifications.

Register filter expressions with the messaging infrastructure so filtering can be pushed closer to the source, cutting wasteful network traffic while keeping routing control with the subscriber, recognizing that infrastructure selectors and hierarchical channel names are less expressive than a full Message Filter.

Choose broadcast-and-filter versus a Recipient List by the infrastructure and the fraction of interested recipients — a Recipient List wins when recipients are few or far apart — and use a Dynamic Recipient List to give subscribers control with router efficiency, even emulating publish-subscribe on point-to-point-only systems.

Choose among Selective Consumer, Message Filter, and Content-Based Router by who wants the messages and how dynamic the options are — a Selective Consumer leaves messages for others and adapts at runtime, a Message Filter removes what no one wants — and put the selection value in the message header so it can be evaluated without parsing the body.
Choose the router variant to the need — fixed, content-based, or context-based, stateless or stateful — and make routing changeable at runtime via a Control Bus or a self-configuring Dynamic Router.

Use a Dynamic Router that self-configures from destinations' control messages for runtime-flexible predictive routing, persisting its rules to survive restarts and resolving conflicts when multiple destinations claim the same message, including for dynamic service discovery.

Apply Guaranteed Delivery selectively, because persistence buys reliability at a performance and disk cost: use it for critical messages, skip it for high-frequency loss-tolerant data, bound buffering with retry timeouts, disable it during testing, and remember it is resilient to expected outages but never truly 100%.
Prevent message data loss at all three points with persistent queues plus synchronous send, client-acknowledge mode, and an ACID commit with last-participant support.
Account for platform-specific persistence configuration, including that publish-subscribe Guaranteed Delivery only reaches active subscribers unless a Durable Subscriber is used.

On a Publish-Subscribe Channel, subscribe before messages of interest are published or they are missed, and use a Durable Subscriber whose inactive state lets the system retain and redeliver messages published while the subscriber was disconnected.
Use a Messaging Bridge to make two separately built messaging systems act as one, avoiding redesigning applications onto a single system.

Adopt a Message Bus — a common data model, common command set, and messaging infrastructure — to form a distributable service-oriented architecture, preferring it over point-to-point spaghetti or a single intermediary that becomes a bottleneck, and require every participant to share the Canonical Data Model.

Make communication two-way with a pair of Request-Reply messages, choosing the message type by intent, having the requestor specify a Return Address, and carrying a Correlation Identifier on a Point-to-Point reply channel so replies match their requests.

Correlate request and reply explicitly: carry a Return Address in the request header so the replier need not hard-code channels, and set the reply's Correlation Identifier to the request's message ID so the requestor (or its callback processor) can match each reply to its request.

Pair endpoint consumer styles to their roles — a requestor awaiting a single reply may poll while a replier should be event-driven because it cannot predict arrivals — and configure message-reading endpoints to read all properties with the correct formatter.

Know the compatibility of Transactional Clients: they work well with a single Polling Consumer, filters, sequences, and Channel Adapters, but not with Event-Driven Consumers or Message Dispatchers and can cause problems with Competing Consumers, and a consumed message stays available to others until commit.

Make multi-recipient delivery atomic and restartable via a single transaction, a persistent record of who was already sent to, or idempotent receivers, and exploit idempotence to safely resend whenever delivery is uncertain.

Use idempotence as an alternative to distributed transactions for safe retries (making an operation idempotent with metadata such as the triggering message's offset, which assumes replay in the same order, deterministic processing, no concurrent updates, and fencing on failover), and ensure a stateful stream process can recover its state after failure by keeping it remote and replicated, local and periodically replicated, or rebuildable from the input streams.

Decompose and recombine complex flows with Splitter, Aggregator, Resequencer, and Scatter-Gather, reconciling multi-recipient responses in an Aggregator that either waits for all to pick the best or takes the first available to optimize throughput.

Use a Composed Message Processor — split, route sub-messages, then re-aggregate, appearing externally as a single filter — dispatching sub-messages in parallel for throughput and explicitly handling missing or delayed responses by delaying, escalating to a human queue, or resending.

When a Splitter breaks a composite message apart, make each item message self-contained by enriching it with shared context and a correlating key, so stateless consumers need not store context across messages and an Aggregator can later recombine the items.

Weigh processing a split message as independent sub-orders against keeping it unified: independence may be the only option without downstream control but degrades the customer experience when the items depend on each other.
Compose individual patterns into larger patterns to gain an abstraction that hides internal complexity and lets implementation details change without affecting other components.

Treat standards as strengthening rather than replacing patterns, because common interoperable implementations make separate instances of a pattern interoperate and let developers apply the patterns at higher levels of abstraction.

Treat patterns and their code examples as adaptable starting points, not canned solutions; rework every example for your own environment, error handling, and production scaffolding before relying on it.
Rely on patterns outliving technologies: the same architectural decisions and cross-platform experience translate across Java, .NET, and other platforms even as the technologies change.

Produce structures by identifying, connecting, and assigning responsibilities to elements derived from the selected concepts, instantiating each concept type appropriately (customize a reference architecture, adapt a pattern's generic structure, realize a tactic through another concept, configure or extend an external component), aware that one concept may affect multiple structures.

Use a Scatter-Gather to broadcast a request and re-aggregate replies, choosing the Recipient List variant for control or the auction publish-subscribe variant for openness, preparing for partial responses, and using a cascading Aggregator so the slowest responder does not stall everything.

Use an auction-style Scatter-Gather over a Publish-Subscribe Channel with an unknown set of listeners and a timeout-based Aggregator completeness condition behind a synchronous client facade, weighing the confidentiality consequence that public bids are visible to competitors.

Use a Process Manager for non-linear or design-time-unknown flows, having the central hub keep its own state and current position and store intermediate data as a Claim Check, while guarding against the hub becoming a bottleneck and against over-using it where simpler routing suffices.

Avoid integration spaghetti from connecting every application directly; use a central Message Broker in hub-and-spoke style, built internally from the routing patterns, so applications need not be aware of one another.

Treat metadata as a parallel system: extract application metadata via adapters into a central repository to drive translator configuration, recognizing that transformation is needed across File Transfer and RPC as well, not only messaging.

Make applications conform to the Canonical Data Model by changing the internal format (rarely practical), a Messaging Mapper inside custom applications, or an external Message Translator, choosing based on transformation complexity and whether the application source is available.

When integrating via Web services, account for SOAP-over-HTTP being synchronous and unreliable: synchronous calls keep the client quickly informed but burden the server with many concurrent connections and per-call recovery, and choose encoding (literal over obsolete SOAP encoding) and binding (RPC versus Document) deliberately.

Reserve XML-over-HTTP/SOAP for cross-platform communication or firewall traversal (accepting marshalling overhead); use the platform's native remote-call mechanism when both sides share a platform, and prefer an asynchronous, message-based approach over synchronous RPC where you can.

Let a web-services framework or Service Activator act as the message channel so application code contains only business logic, and generate proxies and skeletons from the WSDL so SOAP and messaging concerns stay out of the application.

Design a Service Activator so a single service supports both synchronous and asynchronous invocation across messaging technologies: it handles all messaging details and invokes the service as if synchronous, routes unprocessable messages to the Invalid Message Channel, acts as a Messaging Gateway, and becomes a Transactional Client when the service is transactional.

Choose a service's deployment scope to match its instance-lifecycle needs: request scope for a fresh instance per call, session scope to persist across a client's calls, and application scope for a singleton.

Prefer stateless services so any new instance can process a request identically and no history is lost on failure; only under special circumstances route a client's series of messages to the same instance via sessions or sticky sessions, given the instance-failure and overload risk, and store needed state in clients or an external database.

Encapsulate access to each external service behind a gateway exposing a domain-level interface and events that make no reference to messaging, so callers depend only on the domain interface and heterogeneous providers can be treated uniformly.
Factor common messaging-endpoint behaviour such as receiving requests and sending replies into a reusable base service class so each concrete service overrides only its processing logic.

Define access to an external service through a Gateway implemented as a Separated Interface (not a class) so you can have one implementation that calls the real service and at least one Service Stub loaded via a Plugin, keeping the Service Stub as simple as possible because complexity defeats its purpose.

Harden a production messaging system that examples omit: route errors to a central console via systems-management patterns like the Control Bus, encapsulate consume-process-publish in transactions so a crash does not leave partial work, and use a Message Dispatcher with multiple performer threads for high throughput.

Treat production operation as a first-class challenge: loose coupling makes testing and debugging hard, so monitor at both System Management and Business Activity levels through a Control Bus, toggle optional overhead steps with a Detour, and observe flows with Wire Tap, Message History, and a Message Store.
Treat the message bus as a scalable, fault-isolated component (Y/Z splits, not X) and avoid overcrowding it by publishing only value-justified traffic.

Map between domain objects and messages with a separate Messaging Mapper that neither the objects nor the infrastructure know about, because messages carry only scalar data and not object references or inheritance, and embedding mapping in the domain object couples it to messaging and blocks reuse.

Invoke a Messaging Mapper through events, reduce its boilerplate with reflection or code generation, avoid framework one-to-one auto-serialization by mapping through DTO-like interface objects, and still pair it with a Message Translator so the mapper resolves references and types while the translator handles structural mapping to the Canonical Data Model.

Use Competing Consumers to consume one channel in parallel for load balancing, giving each consumer its own session, while recognizing that the JMS spec does not guarantee this technique's semantics or portability across providers.

Be aware that combining load balancing with redelivery in a traditional AMQP or JMS broker inevitably reorders messages (use a separate queue per consumer when order matters), and that such messaging is transient and destructive because acknowledging deletes a message and a new consumer cannot read messages sent before it registered.

Account for the fragmented standards landscape — bodies differ in openness and intellectual-property policy and many competing WS-* specifications are rarely implemented — when betting a design on a particular standard.

Govern by inception: have the central body innovate faster than business units and supply ready guidance and a reference implementation so new standards are adopted during change without migration cost, never decreeing vaporware, while recognizing IT diversity as a rich-company problem.
Guide technology choices rather than specify them, instructing teams toward a category of solution; specify a concrete technology only when needed to preserve an architecture characteristic.

Favor technical breadth over depth for architects: know many solutions and their trade-offs, keep current with trends, and maintain business-domain knowledge, since decisions are long-lasting and hard to change.

Provide guidance through communicated design principles and graduated decision authority (e.g., by library category), requiring a business justification (not just technical) for technology desires, since making teams effective is the architect's own responsibility.

Hold architects to the eight core expectations (make decisions, continually analyze, keep current, ensure compliance, diverse exposure, business-domain knowledge, interpersonal skills, navigate politics), recognizing leadership is roughly half the role.
Recognize that almost every architecture decision will be challenged, so build the negotiation skills needed to get decisions approved.
Recognize that about half of architect effectiveness is people, facilitation, and leadership skill, and lead by example rather than title to earn respect.

Ride the organizational elevator up and down across many levels to gather implementation feedback and observe the consequences of decisions, and measure an architect's value by how many floors they span rather than how high they travel.
Cultivate comfort with ambiguity as a core architect attribute.

Recognize that guide-style architects depend on strong management support because their impact is subtle, and that effective architects act as 'super glue' combining multiple personas while genuinely understanding the parts they connect.

Develop architects on three balanced legs — skill (applying knowledge to real problems), impact (measurable business benefit), and leadership (advancing the practice through mentoring and sharing) — since missing any one caps their growth.
Assume all architectures become iterative because of unknown unknowns; pair an iterative (Agile) process and matching engineering practices with the chosen architecture style.
Design the architecture to be as iterative as possible so it can change rather than requiring the exactly-correct design on the first attempt.

Reject purely emergent architecture for medium-to-large or complex systems (it has never been observed to work there) in favor of an Iteration 0 approach: run a few ADD iterations up front to choose major patterns, frameworks, and components, then handle changing requirements with time-boxed spikes in a separate branch merged only if successful.
Treat Agile methods and architecture as complementary responses to uncertainty whose value rises with uncertainty, so invest more in architecture in uncertain times rather than abandoning it.
Form one collaborative team across architects and developers with bidirectional communication, because the traditional unidirectional hand-off is why architecture rarely works.

Run risk storming collaboratively (no single architect sees all risk): individual non-collaborative identification, then collaborative consensus focused on disagreements and lone flags, then mitigation.

Treat all architect specializations as equally important and focus on getting them to collaborate, since a locally excellent component is worthless if it solves the wrong problem, duplicates another, or cannot integrate.

Protect architecture characteristics with fitness functions — objective integrity assessments built from existing tools (metrics, monitors, tests, chaos engineering) — run continuously as the system changes.

Achieve quality attributes with well-known patterns and tactics rather than inventing new mechanisms, and treat a violated architecture rule of thumb as a warning sign to investigate, unless the requirements are genuinely unprecedented.

Architect for safety by first identifying safety-critical functions with techniques such as FMEA/hazard analysis and fault tree analysis, then designing detection and mitigation, and re-running hazard or fault tree analysis once the architecture exists because design decisions can introduce new safety vulnerabilities.
Separate development process from engineering practices, and credit DevOps as operations adopting XP-style practices (automation, testing, declarative single source of truth).

Treat DevOps (and DevSecOps where a breach would be costly) as practices that shorten commit-to-production time while keeping quality, relying on cultural and organizational change plus tools and architectural design, with automated testing as the critical, hardest ingredient.

Choose messaging topology by trade-off: pub-sub topics give extensibility and decoupling but weaken data security, contract heterogeneity, and per-consumer scaling; point-to-point queues give the opposite.

Select a modifiability pattern by its coupling profile and tradeoffs: client-server gives low coupling and independent evolution but adds network unpredictability; plug-in/microkernel lets plug-ins evolve independently but eases introducing vulnerabilities; layers give portability and reuse but add a per-layer performance penalty that excessive bridging undermines; publish-subscribe gives loose coupling but reduces determinism, testability, and end-to-end encryption.
Translate business drivers into architecture characteristics (scalability, performance, availability) through domain knowledge and stakeholder collaboration.

Identify driving characteristics early by extracting from domain concerns, requirements, and implicit domain knowledge, translating stakeholder language into engineering terms (e.g., 'millions of users' implies scalability; time-to-market = agility+testability+deployability).

Exploit the architecture as a shared abstraction for stakeholder communication: present it to stakeholders early, because doing so surfaces behavioral and requirements questions and reveals missing or unreasonable requirements.
Translate business needs into technical drivers and fight complexity through harmonization, governance, and retiring obsolete systems, so that IT stays aligned to business purpose.

Keep the driving-characteristics list short: avoid the generic-architecture anti-pattern, have stakeholders pick the top three rather than rank everything, and find the simplest set by asking which characteristic to drop first.

Identify components iteratively: treat the first design as a draft and refine through identify→assign→analyze-roles→analyze-characteristics→restructure, letting characteristics (not just function) drive splits.

Drive architecture-pattern selection from a characteristic-priority match (e.g., for scalability favor event-driven, microservices, or space-based; flag layered's deployment, performance, and scalability risk) while still weighing infrastructure support, team skill, budget, deadlines, and application size, because an architecture is very hard and expensive to change once chosen.
Define characteristics objectively and measurably: decompose composite ones (e.g., agility), measure maxima not just averages, and set performance/K-weight budgets grounded in statistics.

Define architecture characteristics as objective, measurable values, decompose composite characteristics such as agility into measurable contributors, and treat unmeasurability as a sign of a vague definition.

Make governance an architect responsibility and automate it with fitness functions — designed collaboratively, codified into the build to govern important-but-not-urgent concerns (e.g., catching cyclic dependencies in CI rather than at late code review).

Codify governance rules as automated layer/architecture tests (e.g., ArchUnit, NetArchTest) and treat fitness functions like professional checklists that express principles and verify them automatically.
Automate architecture governance with fitness functions instead of relying on error-prone manual reviews, making automation and continuous feedback central to enforcement.
Adopt chaos engineering's stance that failure is a matter of when, not if, and test against simulated production failures to harden the system.

In a system designed to be fault-tolerant, deliberately induce faults (for example randomly killing processes) to continually exercise the recovery machinery and build confidence that real faults are handled.

Accept that some complex adaptive systems cannot be fully tested because behaviors are emergent, so inject faults into the running system in a controlled monitored way (as with Chaos Monkey) and log operational data for later reproduction, focusing on the most severe faults.

Scope architecture characteristics at the architecture-quantum level, not the whole system, because code-level metrics cannot see external dependencies like databases that drive operational characteristics.
Use the architecture-quantum boundary as a shared scope and common language that aligns architects, developers, and operations on coupling, behavior, and deployability.

Scope architecture broadly across network, datacenter, compute, storage, deployment, data, and security, and treat the choice of which components to focus on as itself a significant architectural act.
Define an architecture quantum as an independently deployable artifact with high functional cohesion and synchronous connascence, and use the quantum count to decide monolith versus distributed.

Use the architecture quantum, an independently deployable artifact with high functional cohesion, high static coupling, and synchronous dynamic coupling, as the unit for reasoning about deployability; a monolith deployed as a single unit is by definition a single quantum.
Weigh static coupling, embodied by the architecture quantum, as one of the forces in service-granularity decisions, alongside release cadence, affected services, and engineering practices.

Use a litmus test to separate domain requirements from architecture characteristics: an architecture characteristic is abstract and reusable across applications, whereas anything needing domain knowledge to interpret belongs to the domain.

Separate fitness functions (which validate architecture characteristics) from unit and functional tests (which validate domain criteria); decide which to use by asking whether domain knowledge is required to run the test.
Avoid obsessing over the one true design and shun the Big Ball of Mud: favor simple designs as a defense against unforeseeable long-term consequences, choosing among many least-worst options.
Pursue the least-worst combination of trade-offs rather than a single best design, and objectively assess the trade-offs on both sides of each consequential decision.

Voluntarily restrict the design vocabulary to a small set of proven solutions (tactics, patterns, reused and off-the-shelf elements), seeking novel unprecedented designs only when existing proven solutions are insufficient, because discipline yields simpler, more analyzable, more interoperable designs.

Do not reinvent the wheel: make the major design activity identifying, selecting, combining, and adapting existing design concepts to the key drivers, drawing on best-practice catalogs (broad but uneven quality), your own experience (fast but risking the familiar-hammer bias), and peers' knowledge through brainstorming.

Select among alternative design concepts with a table of each alternative's pros, cons, and cost against the drivers (optionally a SWOT analysis), respecting constraints that rule out alternatives and the fact that earlier selections can restrict later ones through incompatibilities.

When two design alternatives do not differ dramatically in consequences, choose one and move on rather than seeking certainty about the best choice, and staff evaluations with people highly skilled in the domain and quality attributes who also have strong facilitation skills.
Require every meaningful architectural decision to have visible downsides, since an option presented with no downsides is unlikely to be meaningful, and do not measure architects by decision count.

Minimize early irreversible decisions, because the project's start is the time of highest ignorance, and instead use flexible, modular designs that localize later change while recognizing that up-front-decision pressure often comes from process and vendors, not technical need.

Treat service-based architecture as a pragmatic distributed style: separately deployed coarse-grained domain services over a shared database with an API-access facade per service, using ACID within a service, avoiding interservice communication, and adding an API gateway for external exposure and cross-cutting concerns.

Control database change in service-based architecture by logically partitioning the database with federated per-domain entity libraries (never one shared entity library), locking common entity objects to the database team, and federating UI/database by domain across network zones.

Recognize service-based architecture's profile: domain-partitioned, high agility/testability/deployability and high fault tolerance from self-contained services, cheap and simple among distributed styles, and a strong DDD fit — accepting that coarse services trade smaller blast-radius isolation for stronger data integrity.

Add a separate Service Layer or a separate Domain Model only when warranted: a Domain Model is less worthwhile for smaller systems, and splitting Service Layer from the domain is occasionally useful rather than mandatory (respected designers disagree).

Keep application-specific logic out of domain object classes and the data-source layer, encapsulating it in a dedicated higher Service Layer that scripts application logic while delegating domain logic to domain objects, and combat duplication in its scripts by delegating to reusable Gateways via a Layer Supertype.

Treat distributed-architecture tools such as sagas, an enterprise service bus, Kafka, or orchestration as context-dependent trade-offs rather than silver bullets, and avoid apples-to-oranges comparisons between them.

Design services to expose application-specific APIs that permit only predetermined inputs and outputs (providing encapsulation), make each service independently deployable and evolvable so old and new versions run simultaneously with compatible encodings, and favor REST built on HTTP principles over SOAP's heavy, tooling-dependent stack that has fallen out of favor.
Coordinate multi-service workflows with orchestration (central mediator) or choreography (no central coordinator), choosing per the coupling and control needed.

Match the event-mediator implementation to orchestration complexity — integration hubs for simple flows, a BPEL engine for sophisticated orchestration, a BPM for very large or human-in-the-loop processes — because mismatching the tool to the need is a recipe for failure.

In broker topologies, have each processor advertise what it did (events that may be ignored) to gain architectural extensibility, treating processing like a relay race; in mediator topologies use domain-grouped mediators and route every event through a simple mediator that classifies and delegates by complexity.

Select the event-driven topology by orchestration need: use the mediator topology when an event has multiple steps needing central orchestration, and the broker topology when the flow is simple and no central orchestration is wanted.

In the mediator topology keep the mediator orchestration-only (it knows the steps, not the business logic), make each event processor a self-contained single-task component, and prefer message topics for processing events so multiple processors can react.

Summarize event-driven architecture's profile as high agility, deployment, performance, and scalability but low testability and ease of development, and note the broker topology deploys more easily than the mediator because the mediator is coupled to its processors.

Use space-based architecture for high, unpredictable, high-concurrency load by removing the database as a synchronous constraint: keep data in replicated in-memory grids in processing units, drive elasticity with a deployment manager, and write back asynchronously via data pumps so units never touch the database directly.

Decouple space-based processing from storage with a data abstraction layer (transformation in data readers/writers), invoke data readers only on full-cache-crash, redeployment, or archive reads, and support a hybrid cloud-app/on-prem-database topology.

Adopt the space-based architecture (replicated in-memory data grids, no central database, dynamically started/stopped processing units) for extreme and variable concurrent load, structuring it as processing units plus virtualized middleware and splitting into multiple processing units by functional area for larger applications.

Apply space-based architecture to smaller, variable-load web applications (e.g., social or auction sites) rather than large operational relational-database systems; include an optional datastore for the initial grid load and asynchronous persistence, and partition volatile versus non-active data to shrink each processing unit's in-memory footprint.

Adopt a shared-nothing distributed architecture with caution rather than reflexively, because the database cannot hide its constraints and trade-offs and it can limit data-model expressiveness, and remember that data is distributed in two complementary ways: replication (copies on several nodes for redundancy and performance) and partitioning (splitting data across nodes).

Choose caching per data nature rather than one model: replicated for small, static, low-update, performance/fault-tolerance-critical data; distributed for large, dynamic, high-update, consistency-critical data; avoid near-cache in space-based architecture; expect higher cost overall.

Use a collaborative distributed cache so one node's result benefits all and no single failure threatens availability; replicate frequently-read, rarely-changed data to every node since cache replication can be lazy.

Manage resources even when demand is fixed: trade one resource for another (cache versus regenerate), add resources when that is the cheapest immediate win, introduce concurrency to cut blocked time, and maintain multiple copies of computation or data (with a consistency or caching strategy) to reduce contention.

Size microservices by purpose, transactions, and choreography rather than by the 'micro' label, iterating to the right granularity, and keep all interesting logic inside bounded contexts (the API layer is optional and must not orchestrate).

Separate microservice operational concerns (which benefit from coupling) from domain logic via the sidecar/service-mesh pattern and service discovery for elasticity, and use protocol-aware heterogeneous interoperability to fit correct-scale technology to each narrow problem.

Coordinate microservices with choreography by default (decoupled, symbiotic with broker EDA) and avoid cross-service transactions — they violate decoupling and signal too-fine granularity; if unavoidable, use the saga pattern sparingly.

Make service-component granularity the central microservices design decision: avoid too-coarse components (which lose the pattern's benefits) and too-fine components (which force orchestration and drift toward heavyweight SOA); treat UI/API-layer orchestration or inter-service calls to serve one request as a signal of wrong granularity or partitioning.

Select the microservices topology by access style — API REST-based for fine-grained API services, application REST-based for low-to-medium business apps with UI screens, centralized messaging for larger apps needing sophisticated transport — and keep any central message broker transport-only and clustered/federated, never an SOA-style orchestrator.
Expect microservices to rate high on agility, deployment, testability, scalability, and ease of development, but low on performance because of its distributed nature.

When adopting bounded-context microservices, plan for transactionality and data as first-class architectural concerns, because moving the database inside the service boundary turns data concerns into architecture concerns.

Apply the microservice pattern of independently deployable, usually stateless services that communicate only through interfaces with acyclic dependencies and a discovery service, to cut time to market and ease scaling, while accepting its tradeoffs: network and discovery overhead, weakness for distributed transactions, and the hard problem of right-sizing service responsibilities.

Select an architecture style contextually: use domain/architecture isomorphism to match shape to problem, recognize microservices depends on DevOps automation, and accept that style preferences shift with ecosystem, capabilities, and external factors.

Do not assume that adopting microservices, frameworks, or off-the-shelf infrastructure removes the need for architectural reasoning; the architect must still reason about the resulting and emergent quality attributes, which are prone to weakest-link and composition problems.

Record decisions as ADRs (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, plus Compliance and Notes): state the decision affirmatively, emphasize why over how, capture impacts and trade-offs, define governance, keep each as its own linked record, use RFC-with-deadline to avoid analysis paralysis, escalate by cost/cross-team/security, and use ADRs to justify standards.
Document each architecture decision in an ADR that captures Context (problem and alternatives), Decision (and its justification), and Consequences (and the trade-offs considered).

Continually analyze architecture risk with a two-dimensional impact×likelihood matrix, build filtered risk assessments accumulated by criteria and domain with unambiguous direction notation, and always rate unproven/unknown technology as the highest risk.

Treat risk mitigation as the most important risk-storming activity, including developers/tech leads, running it continuously (after major features or each iteration), reusing the matrix for Agile story risk, and mitigating uncontrollable external-system risk via published SLA/SLO.

Scale evaluation effort to risk exposure and tolerance like an insurance policy, since the impact of a risk event scales with system cost and safety-criticality and the probability of a bad architecture is higher for unprecedented systems and teams without deep domain experience.

Distinguish the ATAM's core findings: an architectural risk is a decision that may lead to undesirable consequences (risks are the primary output), a non-risk is a decision deemed safe, a sensitivity point markedly affects a quality response, a tradeoff point affects two responses oppositely, and risk themes are systemic weaknesses that threaten business goals.

Present (not just document) by manipulating time: stitch slides with subtle transitions, build information incrementally to use both verbal and visual channels (avoid the Bullet-Riddled Corpse), distinguish infodecks from presentations, and use the invisibility pattern to refocus on the speaker.
Put substance in presentations — alternatives, differences, principles, and interactions — with detailed code or diagrams as handouts rather than crammed onto slides.

Lead the team by setting the right-sized box of constraints — neither control-freak (overly fine-grained, stealing the art of programming) nor armchair (disconnected, useless high-level diagrams) — identifying components/operations/interactions while leaving internal design to developers, and removing roadblocks.

Make diagrams self-explanatory like a user interface needing no legend, read team-produced drawings for what they reveal about the team's thinking, and treat 'this is wrong' as a valuable, iterative signal of a hidden understanding gap.

Use checklists for non-sequential, error-prone, frequently-skipped processes (developer code-completion, unit/functional testing, software release), keeping them small, stating obvious steps, automating items out, and using the Hawthorne effect to ensure compliance.

Reduce systematic software faults through many small measures (carefully examining assumptions and interactions, thorough testing, process isolation, allowing crash-and-restart, production monitoring, and continuous self-checking of guarantees), recognizing that poor error handling causes many critical bugs.

Build operability in through testing at all levels (with automated tests especially for rare corner cases), fast recovery from error (quick config rollback, gradual code rollout, tools to recompute data), and detailed telemetry of performance metrics and error rates for early warning and diagnosis.
Treat high-quality production processes (code inspections, pair programming, solid requirements reviews) as a first-class fault-prevention measure alongside runtime availability tactics.

Treat negotiation as a core skill and negotiate with stakeholders by decoding buzzword grammar, gathering information and translating vernacular into concrete terms, raising cost/time only as a last resort, and using divide-and-conquer to qualify demands.
Before any negotiation, gather as much information as possible and translate vague vernacular into concrete, grounded terms.

Negotiate with developers by earning respect rather than dictating (avoid Ivory Tower): provide and state the justification first, drop commanding 'you must' language, and let a disagreeing developer arrive at the solution themselves.
Resolve architect-to-architect disputes by demonstration over discussion (run a comparison in a production-like environment) and by staying calm and non-personal, pausing when heated.
Use an options model to resolve architect-versus-project-manager disputes by reducing them to differences in time horizon and input parameters.

Fight accidental complexity: distinguish it from essential complexity, apply the 4 C's (communication, collaboration, clarity, conciseness), and stay pragmatic-yet-visionary by isolating the real bottleneck before adopting elaborate theoretical solutions.
Resist adding flexibility or abstraction speculatively; complexity introduced for a future that may not arrive can make the system harder to evolve and delays delivery of its business benefits.

Protect time for the team by controlling meetings (qualify invites with why/agenda, attend only relevant parts, minimize meetings you call, respect developer flow) and by sitting with or regularly walking among the team.

Treat meetings as costly synchronization points: avoid them as the default interaction, never use status meetings, distribute material beforehand, and resist 'just in case' calendar blocking that worsens throughput.

Sustain a career through continuous learning: apply the 20-minute rule first thing daily, avoid technology bubbles, maintain a technology radar (hold/assess/trial/adopt), diversify the technology portfolio, leverage weak links, and build skill through deliberate practice — remembering there are only trade-offs, not right answers.
Treat rational, disciplined decision-making as the key lever that converts skill into impact, while never letting it substitute for the underlying technical knowledge.

Default to the layered (n-tier) architecture as a general-purpose starting point when the best-fit pattern is still unknown, but expect a monolithic tendency with low agility, deployment ease, performance, and scalability.
Recommend the layered pattern where testability and ease of development matter most and where deployment cadence, performance, and scalability are not primary concerns.
Default to running all layers on the server: it confines deployment, eases upgrade and maintenance, and avoids desktop synchronization and compatibility burdens.

Make the microkernel (plug-in) architecture the first choice for product-based applications and for any application released like a versioned product with pluggable features, refactoring later only if requirements outgrow it.
Structure microkernel systems as a minimal core plus stand-alone plug-ins, keeping plug-ins independent of one another with minimal inter-plug-in communication to avoid dependency issues.

Have the microkernel core discover plug-ins through a registry, and for third-party plug-ins insert an adapter to your standard contract and version contracts from the start, so the core needs no per-plug-in specialized code.

Exploit the microkernel pattern's support for evolutionary, incremental design (a stable core extended over time) and its ability to be embedded within another pattern to isolate a volatile area of an application.

Expect the microkernel architecture to rate high on agility, deployment (hot-deploy at runtime), testability, and performance (trim to needed features) but low on scalability and ease of development due to contract, registry, and granularity complexity.

Recognize the scaling-bottleneck cascade in standard web tiers — load moves from web server to application server to database, with the database the final limit — and prefer solving extreme or variable scalability architecturally over scaling the database or retrofitting caching into a non-scalable design.
Most content is static, so serve it from a lightweight, single-purpose server segregated from dynamic content, allowing each to scale independently.

Apply performance and scalability patterns for their effects and costs: a service mesh sidecar offloads cross-cutting concerns at the cost of extra processes; a load balancer hides server failures and smooths latency but must be fast and is a potential bottleneck so replicate it; a throttler keeps services in a sweet spot but its logic must be fast; map-reduce parallelizes large divisible data sets only.

Build space-based architecture on four virtualized-middleware roles: a messaging grid routing each request to an available processing unit, a data grid keeping every processing unit's in-memory data identical via fast asynchronous replication, an optional processing grid orchestrating cross-unit requests, and a deployment manager that adds/removes units by load to deliver variable scalability.

Remember that space-based ('cloud') processing units and middleware can run on local servers rather than only PaaS, and that products vary widely in cost and data-replication capability — establish concrete goals and needs before selecting a product.
Choose an architecture from the specific problems of the system at hand; distrust any blanket 'always do this' advice because no single architecture fits all enterprise applications.
Treat each architecture problem as potentially novel and resist silver-bullet solutions, because prior blog or forum answers rarely transfer to your exact organizational context.
Choose architecture deliberately, because every system has one and letting it happen by default produces a Big Ball of Mud, so fatalism is not a strategy.

Structure enterprise applications into at least three layers — presentation, domain (business logic), and data source — using the lightest separation mechanism (subroutines, then classes, then packages) the application's complexity warrants.

Recognize that data-intensive applications are assembled from standard building blocks (databases, caches, search indexes, stream processing, batch processing) and match each need to the block suited to it.
Enforce the layer dependency rule: domain and data-source code must never call into presentation, so the UI can be substituted or changed without deep ramifications.
Keep domain decisions in the domain layer and let presentation choose only how to display the result (e.g., the domain decides whether sales are improving; presentation decides the colour or chart).

Treat mediating layers such as Application Controller (between presentation and domain) or Data Mapper (between domain and data source) as optional extras: start from the three base layers and add a mediating layer only when a base layer becomes too complex.

Optimize performance through a disciplined, measurement-driven process: get the system running, instrument it, measure before and after every change, and treat all performance advice as unproven until measured on your own configuration.

Re-measure and re-verify optimizations after any significant configuration change (VM, hardware, or database upgrade), since such changes can invalidate prior performance facts or turn a past optimization into a regression.

Treat general performance rules as guidance only: always profile against your specific database and data and reserve dedicated tuning time, because caching behaviour and exceptions vary by environment.

Architect for performance up front (for example with an enlargeable resource pool) rather than fixing it afterward, and instrument the system by logging timing to find where time is actually spent, optimizing only the critical portions.
Use precise performance vocabulary — distinguish response time, responsiveness, latency, throughput, efficiency, capacity, and scalability — when stating performance goals or diagnosing problems.
Set explicit performance goals and benchmark candidate platforms on your own hardware and workload before choosing, because measured throughput directly sets machine count.

Use throughput as the performance measure for batch systems and response time for online systems, and distinguish response time (what the client sees, including network and queueing delays) from latency (the duration a request waits to be handled).

Specify performance requirements as scenarios whose event arrival is periodic, stochastic, or sporadic and whose measures include latency, throughput, unsatisfied-request count, jitter, and resource utilization.

For enterprise systems, prefer building for horizontal (hardware) scalability over raw capacity or software efficiency when adding servers is cheaper than adding programmers or optimizing for weaker hardware.

Treat portability as minimizing and isolating platform dependencies (ideally behind a virtual machine), variability as supporting a preplanned set of variants (especially valuable in product lines), and scalability as effectively utilizing added resources whether scaling out (horizontal/elasticity) or up (vertical).

Scale services by their tradeoffs: vertical scaling needs no redesign but is capped by the largest instance, while horizontal scaling runs multiple copies behind a load balancer (the maintain-multiple-copies tactic); make the load balancer the client-facing address so clients are resilient to instance count and address changes.
Pick the smallest set of tools you can while recognizing that different tools suit different purposes; a tool built for a different kind of application can hinder more than help.
Define the size and scope of the problem before building a solution, and do not default to the tool that is already there — match the tool to the problem.
Deliver software iteratively: release something useful to users as early as possible rather than waiting for a complete system, and actively simplify to turn a large project into a small one.

Build infrastructure and application functionality hand in hand through a walking skeleton that contains initialization, communication, data-sharing, resource-access, error-reporting, and logging but minimal application logic, growing it end-to-end to surface problems early.

Use your influence to ensure early releases tackle the most challenging quality attribute requirements so no architectural surprises appear late, and choose the right amount of up-front work at the project's sweet spot driven mainly by project size plus functional complexity, demanding qualities, volatility, and distribution.
Prefer a web presentation and adopt a rich client only when you must, because web front ends avoid client-deployment problems and are increasingly capable.

Treat presentation as relatively independent of the lower layers: prefer an HTML browser interface if you can get away with it and a rich client only if you cannot, with Model View Controller underneath, and pick controllers and views (Page vs Front Controller, Template vs Transform View) by site nature and team tooling.
If domain logic must run on the client, keep all of it in one place; never split domain logic across client and server, because you then no longer know where any piece of logic lives.

Keep request-specific domain logic out of the Application Controller: because the domain/application boundary is murky a few such cases may live there, but when the logic recurs in many places drive it from the Domain Model instead.

Keep all code in a single process (one node, or replicated across a cluster) and do not separate layers into distinct processes unless you absolutely must, because distribution degrades performance and forces extra patterns like Remote Facade and Data Transfer Object.
To use multiple processors, prefer clustering: put all classes in a single process and run multiple copies of that process across nodes, so every call stays local and fine-grained.

Treat distribution, explicit multithreading, the object/relational impedance mismatch, multiplatform development, and extreme performance needs as complexity boosters that each carry high build-and-maintain cost; adopt each only when genuinely required.
Treat reliability, scalability, and maintainability as the primary design goals even for mundane applications, and sacrifice reliability only as a conscious, explicit cost trade-off.

Expect to rethink the architecture on roughly every order-of-magnitude increase in load, because no architecture is one-size-fits-all (each is specific to its application's load assumptions), and avoid over-engineering for hypothetical future load since wrong load assumptions make the effort wasted or counterproductive.

Select the domain-logic pattern (Transaction Script, Table Module, or Domain Model) primarily by domain-logic complexity: Transaction Script for simple logic, Domain Model as complexity rises, since simple approaches hit a wall where each new feature gets exponentially harder.

Because domain-logic complexity cannot be measured numerically, make the structuring choice as an experienced judgment call from initial requirements analysis, and weight it toward Domain Model when the team is already strong with that approach.

Invest upfront thought in the domain-logic choice because it is hard to change later; if Transaction Script proves wrong, refactor toward Domain Model, but reverting from Domain Model to Transaction Script is rarely worthwhile unless you can also simplify the data source layer.

If you adopt a Domain Model, make it dominant rather than mixing in use-case (Transaction Script) controllers, because such controllers encourage duplicated code; you may still mix patterns deliberately where parts of the system are genuinely simpler.

Make the domain-logic approach (Transaction Script, Table Module, or Domain Model) the central enterprise design decision, driven mainly by domain-logic complexity and secondarily by the difficulty of the database connection.

Match the domain-logic pattern to complexity: Transaction Script for simple logic (its cost multiplies exponentially as logic grows), a Domain Model for genuinely complex logic (needs real skill and brings a messy relational connection), and Table Module as a relational-friendly middle ground (especially strong on .NET).

Understand Transaction Script as organizing all domain logic for one system transaction primarily as a single procedure that calls the database directly or through a thin wrapper, factoring common subtasks into shared subprocedures, with the benefit that each script need not worry about what other transactions are doing.

Watch Transaction Script's failure mode of duplicated code across transactions as business logic grows, and because refactoring a Transaction Script design into a Domain Model is harder than it should be, choose a Domain Model early when you expect the domain logic to become complex.
Use Table Module only when the environment supplies strong Record Set tooling (e.g., COM/.NET); with such tooling prefer it over Transaction Script, and without it do not bother with Table Module.

Separate database logic from a Transaction Script even in the simplest applications, choosing Row Data Gateway or Table Data Gateway, with strong Record Set tooling tilting you toward Table Data Gateway.
On .NET default to Table Module because the platform tooling orbits the data set acting as a Record Set, reserving Transaction Script for the very simplest cases.

Use Table Module to package data with behavior over a relational-friendly backing structure (a Record Set from a SQL call), letting its structure follow the virtual tables the application perceives (views and queries), not strictly the physical tables.

Implement a Table Module as an instance initialized with a record set rather than as static methods, which enables specialization through inheritance and lets you test it by building a Record Set in memory without going to the database.

Use a Row Data Gateway as an object that exactly mimics a single record (one field per column) and hides all data-source access, containing only database-access logic and no domain logic (domain logic would make it an Active Record); it pairs well with Transaction Script by factoring reusable database access.

Use Record Set together with Table Module when your environment relies on the Record Set as its common data structure: fetch a Record Set, pass it to a Table Module to calculate derived information, to the UI for display and editing, back to the Table Module for validation, then commit the updates.

Add a Service Layer as the application's API over a Domain Model or Table Module — a natural home for transaction control and security described per method — but keep it as thin as possible (or omit it), adopting it only when the application demands it.

Make a Service Layer operation responsible for coordinating and atomically transacting the application's full response to a use case (for example validation plus notifying other people and integrated applications), which can be far from trivial.

Match the persistence mechanism to the Domain Model's richness: use Active Record for a simple model that mirrors the tables, and Data Mapper for a rich model, since Active Record breaks down once one-to-one class/table mapping fails or you need inheritance and database-free domain tests.

Build the Domain Model without regard to the database — beware a model shaped like the schema — and treat the schema purely as a way to persist object data; use Data Mapper for maximum flexibility, or Active Record only when an isomorphic schema genuinely makes sense.

For a Domain Model choose the data-source pattern by complexity: Active Record when simple, Data Mapper (ideally with a mapping tool) when complex, and Unit of Work as the focal point for concurrency control.

Do not shield a Domain Model with a Row Data Gateway (three data representations is one too many): use Active Record for simple mappings and Data Mapper for complex ones, keeping Row Data Gateways mirroring the database structure.

Use Data Mapper to let the database schema and object model evolve independently (most commonly with a Domain Model, so you can ignore the database while designing and testing the model); because its price is an extra layer, gate on complexity: simple logic needs neither Domain Model nor Data Mapper, never use Data Mapper without a Domain Model, but a simple Domain Model over a developer-controlled database may use Active Record and refactor to a mapping layer as complexity grows.

Budget object-relational mapping as a large, ongoing cost (anecdotally ~a third of programming effort that persists through maintenance), and seriously consider buying a mature O/R mapping tool for a Domain Model rather than hand-building the layer.

Bridge object references and relational keys with Identity Field, Identity Map, and Foreign Key Mapping: store each object's key, look up by key on read, and wire references from foreign keys, falling back to a database fetch or Lazy Load when the key is not already in memory.

Treat repetitive mapping code as a design smell: factor out the common behaviour or adopt Metadata Mapping (a metadata description driving code generation or reflection), which is why mature commercial O/R tools are metadata-based and enable Query Object and Repository.

Adopt a Repository to concentrate query-construction code in one place and minimize duplicate query logic (important with many domain classes or heavy querying), gaining a clean one-way dependency from domain to data mapping and a persistence layer that looks like an in-memory collection of domain objects.
Use an Identity Map to record every row read so the same row is never loaded into two in-memory objects; treat correct identity as its primary purpose and caching as only a secondary benefit.
Use Identity Field to store the relational primary key inside the in-memory object, maintaining the object-to-row correspondence required in order to write data back.

Read efficiently: pull back multiple rows at once, never issue repeated queries on the same table, and prefer joins to load several tables together — but limit to about three or four joins per query before performance suffers.

Gather data from multiple tables in a single joined query (a multitable find) rather than one query per table, because each SQL call is a slow remote call; and when loading a referenced object from the join, check the Identity Map first so an already-loaded object is reused rather than duplicated.

Avoid the N+1 query problem (loading N objects when each needs a separate query for its association turns into N+1 queries, such as 101 for a hundred employees and their skills) by using a multitable join, but because that optimization is more awkward, apply it only where needed and spend your energy on the slow, important queries.

Prefer separate finder objects over static find methods so database operations stay substitutable (e.g., replaceable by a Service Stub in tests), and run queries at the start of a unit of work since finders see database state, not unsaved in-memory objects.
Prefer separate finder objects over static find methods on a Row Data Gateway so finders remain polymorphic and substitutable across different data sources.
Do not depend on collection ordering across persistence: use unordered sets or apply an explicit sort per query, since arbitrary order is hard to maintain in a relational store.

In a column store, impose a sort order an entire row at a time (never per column) to act as an index chosen from common queries, which also boosts compression by forming long runs on the first sort key, and consider storing the data sorted several different ways across the replicas you keep for fault tolerance so each query uses the best-fitting order.

Control write ordering for referential integrity: defer integrity checks to transaction end if the database supports it; otherwise order writes by topological/hardcoded table order to satisfy per-write checks and reduce deadlock rollbacks.

Avoid manually ordering updates for referential integrity by configuring the database to check integrity only at commit (most databases allow it, with no good reason not to); otherwise let the Unit of Work sort update order, and always edit tables in the same fixed sequence (held in the Unit of Work) to reduce deadlocks.

Separate the two requirements that consistency conflates, timeliness (an up-to-date view, whose violations are temporary and resolve by waiting) and integrity (absence of corruption, whose violations are permanent and need explicit repair), and prioritize integrity over timeliness in most applications because a timeliness lapse is merely annoying while an integrity lapse such as money charged but not paid is catastrophic; note that ACID transactions provide both but event-based dataflow decouples them, with integrity preserved by exactly-once semantics.

Where the cost of an apology is acceptable, adopt loosely interpreted constraints by writing optimistically and checking the constraint after the fact (compensating for violations through apology workflows) rather than checking every constraint before writing, which enables coordination-avoiding data systems that maintain strong integrity without atomic commit, linearizability, or synchronous cross-partition coordination, such as a multi-leader deployment replicating asynchronously across datacenters with synchronous coordination introduced only where recovery is impossible.

Use a Serialized LOB to store a clustered object group as one column (e.g., XML) to avoid many small calls for hierarchic structures, but only when you never need to query the parts, and not so widely that the database degenerates into a transactional file system.

Pick a Serialized LOB form by trade-offs: a BLOB is simplest and most space-efficient where the platform auto-serializes but is binary, opaque to casual viewing, and most seriously suffers versioning problems when the class changes, while a CLOB is human-readable but larger, may need a custom parser, and is slower; XML removes the parser and standardization problems at a verbosity (space) cost, and a zipped XML BLOB trades readability back for space.

Beware identity and duplication with a Serialized LOB: do not embed a shared, updatable LOB (such as customer details) in another table (such as order), which copies the data per row; place the LOB in its own table so many rows can link to it, and ensure its data is reachable only from the single owning object, embedding it only when you deliberately want a point-in-time snapshot.

Use Serialized LOB only for a slice of the object model that will not be queried via SQL from outside the application, because it works poorly when outside objects must reference objects buried inside it, and its main disadvantage is that you cannot query its internal structure with SQL.
Note that structures suitable for a Serialized LOB are often also suitable for a separate denormalized reporting database, into which the LOB can be transformed into table structures.

Choose an inheritance-mapping strategy by trading data duplication against access speed: default to Single Table Inheritance for simplicity and refactoring resilience, and reach for Class or Concrete Table Inheritance as wasted-column or access pressures demand, mixing strategies only when justified and consulting DBAs.

For Class Table Inheritance, give each class its own mapper that handles only that class's table (chaining to the superclass mapper via base calls) with a top-level mapper dispatching by type code on find and by runtime type on update, insert, and delete; cache query results in an in-memory data set to access table data cheaply (or join across all the hierarchy's tables), and insert in two stages: create the blank rows, then let per-class save methods populate them.

Treat database connections as expensive resources: tie each connection to its transaction (open on begin, close on commit/rollback), close as soon as you are done, and do not rely on garbage collection to close them.

Keep all data manipulation inside transactions so the transaction manager handles the most dangerous concurrency problems, but manage offline concurrency (across multiple transactions) explicitly, since no single system transaction can cover it.

Keep transactions as short as possible for throughput and, as a general rule, never let a single system transaction span multiple requests; open the transaction late (at first write) only when contention is heavy or business transactions span requests, accepting the inconsistent-read exposure.

Know what each transaction locks: too many row locks make the database escalate to a table lock that excludes everyone, so avoid a single shared 'object' table or Layer Supertype table that becomes a lock-escalation magnet.

Usually wrap a whole Transaction Script in a single system transaction, except when one request reads data for editing and a later request saves it, where Optimistic Offline Lock is almost always the best choice.

Split request handling from response formatting with Model View Controller: use a script/controller to interpret the request and a server page to format the response, keeping domain models completely separate so presentation is easy to change and domain logic easy to test.

Have a Page Controller handle a request by creating the necessary model objects, placing the data the view needs into the HTTP request, and forwarding to the view (putting the common forwarding on a superclass), and recognize that its main coupling to a Template View is the request-parameter names used to pass objects.

Use Transform View to render the model's data into HTML as a transformation that walks the domain data and writes HTML per recognized element type, recognizing that, unlike an output-organized Template View, a Transform View is organized around separate per-element transforms dispatched by a simple loop, so its rules can be arranged in any order without affecting the output.

Add an Application Controller only when the machine controls screen flow and navigation order; you do not need one when the user is free to reach any screen in any order (test: machine-in-control ⇒ needed; user-in-control ⇒ not).

Use an Application Controller when there are definite rules about the order pages are visited and state-dependent view choices, and skip it when any screen can be visited in any order; treat having to make similar changes in many places whenever the flow changes as the signal to introduce one.

Keep programming logic out of the page structure in a Template View (delegate to a helper object), because embedded logic tends toward messy, unmaintainable pages; use Transform View when domain data is XML, and Two Step View only when screens share a common logical structure.

Avoid programming logic (scriptlets) in server pages, because a page is a poor program module that loses structural and modular features, blocks designers and nonprogrammers from editing it, and makes it too easy to mingle layers and duplicate domain logic; instead give each page a regular helper object holding the real logic so the page stays a pure Template View.

Choose optimistic vs pessimistic locking by conflict frequency and severity: prefer optimistic (conflict detection at commit — better concurrency, easier to implement) when conflicts are rare or low-consequence, and pessimistic (conflict prevention) when a late-discovered conflict is painful for users.

Treat deadlock as the characteristic risk of pessimistic locking, and for enterprise applications prefer very simple, conservative schemes (e.g., acquire all locks up front plus a timeout), accepting some unnecessary victims, because missing a deadlock scenario is far worse and 'deadlock-proof' schemes are easy to get wrong.
